subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF SUPPORT FOR PRINCIPLE OF NON-INTERVENTION IN INTERNAL AFFAIRS OF ANGOLA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On January 5, 1973 this House approved a motion proposed by the government asserting the strong support of this chamber for the principle of non-intervention in the internal affairs of other countries and censuring a country which appeared to have violated that principle in respect of the Viet Nam conflict.
On the assumption that hon. members on all sides of this House wish to remain consistent in the application of that general principle, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and hopefully supported by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
That this House noted with grave concern the continuation of the civil war in Angola and deplores the large scale intervention by other states in this civil war; is aware of the fact that the war is being prolonged by outside intervention, thereby increasing the suffering of the Angolan people; welcomes the declared intention of the government of South Africa to withdraw its troops from Angola, as it is believed to be doing at this moment, and calls on the government of Cuba to do likewise; urges the MPLA, the FNLA and UNITA to call a ceasefire and to conduct negotiations with a view to reaching a political settlement acceptable to all parties, and requests the government to convey the text of this resolution to all participants in the Angolan civil war including those who are providing arms, munitions and war materiel, and to the United Nations.

speechtext:
I discussed this first at a meeting of premiers which took place about one year ago and got general agreement from all of them that we should, indeed, proceed with the repatriation of the constitution in the course of the next few years. I was talking about the life of this parliament, and I would say there was general agreement that we should concentrate on repatriation and on the formula of amendment rather than re-open the whole series of discussions on jurisdiction under the British North America Act, sections 91 and 92. There was general agreement along the lines that we should attempt to work out a solution which would permit repatriation, without any premier binding himself to such an absolute. That was the thrust of the discussions with which the federal government was encouraged to proceed.
Following that there have been a great number of meetings between federal officials and officials of all provinces, I believe, except one. There have been few discussions at the ministerial level, and certainly no collective ones. At this stage I can only say that it is our hope to find a formula upon which all provinces will agree, and I hope that that will be done, certainly, before the end of this parliament. I am quite determined to see that it does happen.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I will not ask the Prime Minister for disclosure of any details which might be inappropriate at this time. Indeed, I

will even resist asking him if he is wrestling Mr. Bourassa to the ground. Can he indicate generally if he envisages a first ministers' meeting to pursue the discussions taking place at the ministerial level at present? If so, can the Prime Minister indicate, in general terms, when he expects discussions to resume at the first ministers's level, so that, as he said, this problem can be dealt with and this challenge met during the life of this parliament; or, to use another phrase he used during that debate, before we, in this parliament, disappear from the scene?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROGRESS IN FINDING AMENDING FORMULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the best answer is to say that I do not envisage a meeting of first ministers on this subject unless I see the solution in sight. I do not want to put the government of this country, the governments of the provinces and the people of Canada through the long process of expectation, namely, that we can find a formula on which all would agree if such formula is not possible. The House will realize that since 1926, some 50 years, federal and provincial governments have been struggling to bring the constitution back to Canada, and every time this has failed for some reason or other. I would not want to waste the time of parliament or of the premiers by getting them together to embark upon another long series of discussions in order to repatriate the constitution. I am hopeful that the behind-the-scenes discussion going on at the official level will permit us to find a formula which is acceptable. It would mean, of course, confirmation by the premiers and, most important, submission to parliament, for the approbation of such formula.
I appreciate the Leader of the Opposition's discretion in not asking about the details. I think this approach is very helpful. I think I owe it to him to indicate that we are looking at the type of amendment formula which was discussed at Victoria, but not at the whole bag which was discussed at Victoria, in which many other subjects were included. We are looking strictly at the amendment formula or some variation of that.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROGRESS IN FINDING AMENDING FORMULA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a final supplementary question? I think the Prime Minister has already created the expectation, in the sense that he expressed his determination almost one year and a half ago to see an amending formula adopted. Is he encouraged to believe that he will be able to present a formula to the first ministers and to parliament during a reasonable time? I ask this because I would like to see this question settled before I leave parliament which, of course, will be within the end of this parliament. Can the Prime Minister say whether he is encouraged after the discussions that have taken place or, rather, is it a question of a stalemate?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. It pertains to the continued pumping by Eldorado Nuclear each day of hundreds of gallons of water containing uranium and arsenic into Lake Ontario in the Port Hope area. I am addressing my question to the Prime Minister since it was obvious yesterday that the minister responsible is unfamiliar with the situation. Considering that Eldorado Nuclear has confirmed that this is not a casual run-off, as the minister suggested yesterday, but rather that the water is flowing, as I said, at a constant rate of hundreds of gallons per day, and bearing in mind that the federal government itself tabled a report last July indicating that this flow was unacceptable, I should like to ask the Prime Minister, having in mind his expressed concern that measures be taken against pollution, whether he will take steps to bring this to a halt immediately?

speechtext: The general answer, Mr. Speaker, is yes. I would not say I heard about these two specific planes. subsubtopic: VOTE ON RESOLUTION 3414 (XXX) OF DECEMBER 5, 1975 CONCERNING TERRITORIES OCCUPIED BY ISRAEL
speechtext:
1.	Does Canada's negative vote on the United Nations General Assembly resolution December 5, 1975 condemning Israel's continuous occupation of Arab territories imply that Canada recognizes Israeli sovereignty over the territories?
2.	For what reason did the Canadian delegation vote against this resolution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: VOTE ON RESOLUTION 3414 (XXX) OF DECEMBER 5, 1975 CONCERNING TERRITORIES OCCUPIED BY ISRAEL
speechtext:
The intent of U.N. General Assembly Resolution 3414 (XXX) of December 5, 1975, as expressed by the cosponsors was to seek a just and lasting peace in the Middle East. Canada voted against the resolution, without a formal explanation of vote, because we did not think it would in fact make a positive contribution to the achievement of peace in the area. Our principal objection to the resolution was that it presented an essentially unbalanced statement of the situation. It made no specific reference to Security Council resolutions 242 and 338, which remain basic to the establishment of a durable peace and which contain the essential elements necessary for the achievement of this objective. Furthermore, the resolution appealed to all states "to desist from supplying Israel with any military or economic aid" but ignored the military support provided to other states in the area. The resolution also hinted that sanctions should be imposed against Israel, a measure which Canada considers to be totally unwarranted. Even if this were warranted, it would be an infringement on the prerogatives of the Security Council. Canada did not think that the UNGA would serve the aim of achieving a lasting peace in the Middle East by condemning Israel's continued occupation of the territories while remaining silent on other elements in Resolution 242 such as the right of all states in the area to live in peace and security. Our negative vote can in no way be construed as recognition by Canada of any kind of Israeli sovereignty over occupied Arab territories. Indeed, there could not be any such recognition.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to report, as
February 5, 1976

requested by at least one hon. member, and probably others, on the progress which has been made in initiating a dialogue among industrialized countries on the Conference on International Economic Co-operation. I have attended two meetings in Paris as co-chairman of the conference, a function which I share with the Venezuelan minister of state for international economic affairs, Dr. Manuel Perez Guerrero. We have worked together very closely from the start and I want to pay tribute to his wisdom, knowledge and good judgment.
The Conference on International Economic Co-operation is a new venture in international diplomacy bringing together 27 participants-19 developing countries and 8 developed members including the European Community. Seven of the developing countries are members of OPEC, whereas 12 are oil importing countries. The membership of the conference has been selected to be broadly representative of the interests of the world community as a whole with the exception of eastern Europe and China which are not participating.
The use of co-chairmen from the two groups to head the conference and the commissions is a new technique in conferences of this kind. Limited, but representative, membership may ensure that any consensus reached at the conference is broadly acceptable to the international community. It may also make it possible to replace the highly politicized and often sterile debate on international economic problems by a pragmatic and systematic approach to complex questions which cannot be resolved by rhetoric. Limited membership may also be conducive to better understanding, and hence to a more earnest and direct attack on specific issues.
The origins of this conference are diverse and are reflected in its character. What began as a reaction to the quadrupling of petroleum prices in late 1973 has evolved over the past two years into a conference designed to examine many of the world's major economic problems in addition to those associated with energy. The conference will undoubtedly address the various demands for changes in the world's economic system which have been put forward by developing countries in the United Nations. Since the first impact of the oil price rise, Canada has been a consistent advocate of such a consumer-producer dialogue and has in particular advocated including the "innocent victims"-the most seriously affected developing countries- in the dialogue. I am, therefore, particularly gratified that the conference can truthfully be described as a dialogue between developed and developing countries, between producers and consumers of petroleum, and between producers and consumers of other raw materials.
During the coming year the conference will attempt to reach agreement by consensus on a variety of important issues in the fields of energy, raw materials, development and finance. It is my hope that in the process it will make a positive contribution to a new era of international economic co-operation by fostering better understanding and by stimulating ongoing work in other bodies such as UNCTAD, UNIDO, the GATT, the FAO, the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank.
International Economic Co-operation
The ministerial meeting in December which President Giscard d'Estaing opened and which Dr. Perez Guerrero and I chaired brought together ministers from the 27 members of the conference. We agreed on the creation of four commissions: for energy, raw materials, development, and financial affairs. Each consists of 15 members, five representing developed, and ten representing developing members. We agreed on the co-chairmen for each of the four commissions and approved general guidelines regarding the work of the conference.
At a follow-up meeting last week, Dr. Perez Guerrero and I, as conference co-chairmen, together with the eight co-chairmen of the four commissions, reviewed preparations for the work of the commissions. We agreed that each of the commissions should meet five times between now and July, and we made a number of recommendations with respect to the duration of meetings, participation by observers and other procedures. While the initial meetings of the commission will probably deal with organizational and procedural matters, I believe they will quickly move on to substantive questions. A meeting of senior officials from the 27 members may review the progress of the commissions in about five months' time, probably in June. I should qualify that statement by saying that the recommendation has been made by the conference co-chairmen but has not yet been acted upon or agreed to by the participating governments. Of course, it is expected that a ministerial meeting will be held next December to conclude the work of the commissions.
The two co-chairmen of the conference have a particularly sensitive role to play. Although all participants in the Conference on International Economic Co-operation are prepared to approach issues in a positive and co-operative manner, there is a broad range of differing national interests and philosophies among the developed, developing, and OPEC members of the conference. To a degree, it was this very diversity of interests and the consequent difficulty of providing leadership equally responsive to both the group of 8, the developed members, and the group of 19, the developing members, which led to the choice of the two co-chairmen as a technique for organizing the conference. This co-direction of the conference is symbolic of the determination of the member countries to work together and to accept shared responsibility for the results.
Just as Dr. Perez Guerrero and I have a certain responsibility for ensuring that the work of the conference proceeds in an orderly and constructive manner, so the co-chairmen of the commissions have a responsibility for guiding the work of their commissions so that they achieve results which are broadly acceptable to the international community, including those countries which are not members of the conference. As I said, I have been working closely with my co-chairman and I am sure that the co-chairmen of the commissions will also work together constructively.
Canada is a member of two of the four commissions: energy and development. The dialogue in the energy commission may eventually encompass such sensitive issues as oil prices, indexation, and security of supply. We hope that it will lead to increased stability in the international oil market which would facilitate the orderly planning and development of Canada's own energy needs. I also trust

the dialogue will make a real contribution to solving the problems of the developing countries most seriously affected by the rise in oil and other prices.
I am particularly pleased that Canada will participate in the work of the development commission. As you know, Canada has won considerable respect in the third world for its stand on development questions. I can assure the House that Canada will continue this positive approach in the development commission which will probably consider a broad range of issues in such key areas as food and agricultural development, industrial and technological co-operation, trade liberalization, and official development assistance.
Canada is not a member of the raw materials and finance commissions. As they may deal with a number of vital issues such as the stabilization of commodity prices, the stabilization of earnings derived from commodity exports, and international financial questions, we do have a substantial interest in their proceedings. We shall, therefore, be following the work of these commissions closely through our observers in them. We expect to consult frequently and closely with our colleagues in the conference who are participating in these commissions.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by acknowledging the role the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) played in the Conference on International Economic Co-operation. I congratulate him on his role as co-chairman, tell him we support him in his efforts to bring developed and developing nations together, and suggest that his role is constructive. If I am critical about some of his comments, let me add that I am critical in the context of supporting his intention as revealed once again in his speech. His speech was of the same tenor as the one he made to the United Nations on September 3, 1975, when he unveiled Canada's new five-year strategy. There is a difference between presiding and participating. The minister has been pretty good at presiding. That is a role which you, Mr. Speaker, can well appreciate. My party wants to know more about the specifics of Canada's participation in the north-south conference. What are the specifics of our participation?
The origins of the conference began with the quintupling of oil prices charged by OPEC nations. That price rise was a factor in creating worldwide economic disarray and produced a spirit of confrontation at the sixth special session of the United Nations General Assembly. That session gave birth, so to speak, in May, 1974, to a document known as the "New International Economic Order." A process of severe confrontation, about which developed nations entered several reservations, led to the creation of that document. The sixth session was followed by the seventh session in September, 1975, and the spirit of confrontation gave way to a new spirit of consensus.

Canadian participation in the seventh special session was a marked improvement over the sixth session even though we still had some reservations about the specifics called for by the developing nations with reference to the new economic border. The five-year strategy plugged into the new economic order that was reaffirmed at the seventh special session. However, it has been criticized, and I think fairly, as still being too rhetorical, the position on the part of Canada, when in fact the multidimensional approach- which is the code word for describing Canada's new role in international development-is a shift from reliance on aid as an expression of our humanitarian concern, over to the structural changes of trade and monetary reform, the two together, aid and trade, making a multidimensional policy which is at the heart of the five-year strategy of the Canadian government.
This was touched on by the minister in his speech in New York where he said that Canada was prepared to move ahead in commodities, trade liberalization and industrial co-operation. The minister opened up those areas. They are the very areas that the north-south conference has been called to deal with. We are past the stage of rhetoric, past the stage of expressing good intentions.
I reply to the minister today by emphasizing that we are waiting-I would like to say patiently, but I have to say impatiently-for more detail on how Canada is going to participate. There is the interdepartmental committee of officials of various departments of the Canadian government: we know that. There are the subcommittee on international development and the external affairs committee studying this issue at great length. Speaking as a member of that subcommittee, we cannot move too far into the field until we know where Canada will open up the areas of trade liberalization, commodities and industrial co-operation. There are some very hard questions that Canada has to face with respect to meaningful participation as distinct from presiding over a north-south conference.
Many of the nations which form the industrialized and developing group within the North-South Conference are fully cognizant of the urgency of this question. That urgency has been reflected in Canada's own five-year strategy in which we make reference to the fact that 800 million people around the world can expect almost no improvement in their conditions of life for the rest of the decade because of the cyclical poverty which is brought about by economic control systems in trade and commerce which severely disadvantage the developing nations. Therefore, we are pleased that Canada is beginning to move ahead.
I say, parenthetically, that it will be difficult for us to make real progress on the international scene-and I make the plea to the minister with some feeling on the part of Canadians-until we are solidly plugged into this international system for change, the North-South Conference. Canadians must first of all be aware that there is a new, five-year strategy. I can assure the minister that generally speaking Canadians do not even know this strategy exists. It can be criticized. However, Canadians must first recognize that we are now in the process of moving away from just aid to the multidimensional, the structural changes. I think the five-year strategy needs not only implementa-
February 5, 1976

tion but constructive criticism that will help us to participate more meaningfully in the North-South Conference.
A leading Canadian expert on development, Professor Gerald Helleiner, warns that the "rhetoric on co-operation" glosses over serious inadequacies. Canada is actually dragging its feet on such subjects as the SDR-aid link, reducing tariffs and fair sugar prices, and Canadian representation at international conferences has played too much of a protective role for Canada.
Therefore, I ask the minister how we are going to examine positively the idea of negotiating arrangements for a wide range of products under the commodities section of his speech in New York. How are we going to consider deeper tariff cuts and advance implementation on an m.f.n. basis, or other tariff cuts of interest to developing countries unless we move away from rhetoric and begin to bring into parliament and the subcommittee some of the detail of the thinking going on in the interdepartmental committee that is in the normal process of feeding material for the cabinet to consider?
The Canadian government, and the minister in particular, need the continued support they now have. This can only be retained by having us participate in the ongoing development of our own knowledge of the technical complexities of the structural changes in the multinational policy so that we, as members of parliament, can both understand and contribute to it. It will be a great mistake to go on in the way we have been doing, that is to say, to dump onto the scene a policy that came out of-where? Members of parliament did not participate in the creation of this policy. There are many members, particularly in the subcommittee, who want to have this ongoing role of participation.
The minister talked today about the positive approach he wants to bring into the development commission. A positive approach for what, and for whom? Is it for us, for the continuation of our own benefit with the systems of international commerce benefitting the developed nations, which is at the heart of the problem, or a positive approach to changing those systems? If we are going to demand stable oil prices, what will we offer the group of 77 in return? The minister's statement today was, unfortunately, very vague on what he is going to do.
The mood of co-operation that the minister exemplified in his statement and conduct-and for that I again congratulate him-must dominate new international relationships if there is to be any hope of achieving the new order. The five-year strategy warns that "a hostile reaction by the rich will only intensify the mood of the frustration of the majority of the world's population and foster an atmosphere of confrontation of international affairs."
We are in a dilemma. The massive changes of the new economic order cannot be implemented overnight. The developing world cannot, and will not, wait for our beneficence to catch up with reality. There is a note of urgency that must be maintained in the minister's conduct and in his participation, as well as presiding. I will back him on that urgency, provided he continues to make statements that enlarge the Canadian position in a participatory way as to how we can help the developing nations by better commodity pricing and trade liberalization with meaningful industrial co-operation.

As the minister said, this conference is an initiation of a dialogue among industrial and developing countries. The conference, as the minister also mentioned, arose out of OPEC and its quadrupling of petroleum prices. However, it has now gone far beyond a cartel of producer countries: the emphasis has shifted to a consumer-producer dialogue. In the opinion of the government, and I share this opinion, that is a far better approach than existed before. We have already had our attention called by the right hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) to the seventh-

I thought I might in that way give you a boost. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona has referred to the seventh special session of the United Nations, held in September of last year. That session announced a new era of worldwide co-operation under the title of the New International Economic Order. This set up a framework, but it will be a long and arduous task to fit in the details and make the aspirations turn into fact. It is essential for the so-called developed, underdeveloped and developing countries to work together to remove what was described at the special session by the minister himself as gross disparities between conditions in the rich and in the poor nations.
I am pleased that Canada has taken its place on the commission on energy and the commission on development. Obviously, Canada is greatly concerned with the question of energy. We are a major supplier of energy as well as a major consumer of energy; we are deeply concerned about this matter and it is one which should be discussed and dealt with on an international basis. I am particularly pleased that we should be a member of the commission on development, for in my mind development has become the key word, item number one among the international issues affecting Canada and, indeed, the world. I hope, as has already been said, that the subcommittee of the external affairs committee of this House will be used to the full by the minister as a forum of discussion by what is really, now, a non-partisan group in connection with developments arising from the work and the discussions of this commission.
The conference to which I have referred is, of course, only one among many; it is only one instrument of international co-operation. Other steps are needed if the basic requirements of humanity are to be met and a stable world developed. Nevertheless, the conference is an event which is potentially important, and we are glad to promise to the minister our support to help him meet the challenge which is before him as chairman of this commission.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) referred to the needs of third world countries and to stabilization agreements related to commodity prices. Could he indicate succinct-

February 5, 1976
International Economic Co-operation
ly-I know he is able to do so-Canada's position with regard to stabilization agreements? Is Canada prepared to put forward a precise position with regard to such agreements and, if so, what is that position? Has Canada already done so?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
I will reply in general terms, Mr. Speaker. Canada did state at the seventh session of the United Nations that we were in support, or could certainly support, certain elements in the integrated commodity approach and that we were ready, also, in certain circumstances to consider the question of buffer stocks, which is also part of the integrated approach which has been put forward. Beyond this generally positive statement we have not developed a position in detail with regard to commodity agreements, because I believe this would require, particularly within the commission, a good deal of negotiation and discussion.
It is my view that in the course of the dialogue itself a response will be required not only from Canada but from the seven other industrialized countries which are operating as a representative group on behalf of the industrialized world, so to speak. While I am sure each country on the commission must take into account its own national interest, it will be necessary to work out with the other countries in the group, where possible, a common approach. That is how the dialogue has been developing so far.
I would think the area of commodity agreements is one in which the group of eight industrialized countries would be working out a detailed position. However, in general Canada has taken what I consider to be a positive approach toward the question of commodity stabilization. We have not endorsed without question-or, indeed, at all-the concept of indexation, although we do support the general objective of the developing countries, which is to protect their major export earnings, upon which they are so dependent, from the effects of price fluctuations. As a general principle, we would certainly work to bring that about. The precise application of indexation as put forward is extremely difficult, however, and might in some cases even work against the interests of the developing countries.
I believe the value of the dialogue which will take place in these commissions is likely to be the opportunity it provides for countries to discuss questions such as indexation in a practical context apart from the rhetoric which could be associated with them in a more political forum.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Since the purpose of the conference is to reduce the great disparity between the so-called northern developed countries on one hand, and the so-called southern underdeveloped countries on the other, and reduce or eliminate the sense of injustice felt in the underdeveloped countries, thereby, presumably, reducing the threat to peace, and bearing in mind the feeling of the underdeveloped countries that we have all been fooling around with this question-perhaps sincerely, but without much effect, for a number of years-and the feeling of dissatisfaction and expectation which exists, I am disappointed that the hon. gentleman did not tell us whether or not Canada would be taking any initiatives by way of proposals, and what those proposals would be.

Is it the intention of Canada to take some initiatives and to make some proposals, or is it simply to react to what is put forward by other nations on these various commissions? If Canada is taking certain initiatives and will be putting forward certain tangible, if not concrete, proposals in this connection, in what area will they be?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by expressing agreement with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that it would be unfortunate if the conclusion of the conference were to be a feeling of frustration on the part, not only of the developing countries but frustration, I think, would be generally felt if the north-south dialogue produced very little in the way of concrete solutions.
One of my objectives will be to attempt to facilitate the reaching of, if not glamorous or spectacular results, at least limited or visible results which will have justified the dialogue. In saying that, I would mention to the Leader of the Opposition that in the two meetings that have already been held very formidable difficulties have been cleared away, obstacles that up to now have prevented the dialogue from beginning. So the dialogue is now to begin, the framework has been laid out, the work program has been laid out, key players have been identified, agendas or suggested lists of subjects have been proposed, particularly by the group of 19, by the United States, and the commissions will develop their own work program and, presumably, the listing of the subjects.
It is my expectation that Canada will be participating in the dialogue. It will also be making proposals or taking initiatives. I hope Canada will not be a passive participant or partner, but in certain commissions will make proposals that will not only protect our own national interests which are involved in a number of these commissions but which also will help bridge the gap.
I have made it clear that I was not able today to indicate the substance of our proposals; these are under development. Instructions for the opening commissions are now under preparation, but I do not for a moment underestimate the difficulties that a country like Canada will face in taking forthcoming positions on many of these questions. I believe we will face real difficulties. When hon. members rightly underline the necessity for making concessions in the trade field, it must borne in mind that there is no substantial concession that can be made for access to our markets which will not have an appropriate effect on unemployment or production in Canada.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext: Or an inappropriate effect.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext: "Inappropriate" would generally be the word used. It would have an effect on our employment and production. If meaningful adjustments are to take place that will bring benefits to the developing world, they will, in my view, require sacrifices in the developed countries. I do not think we are kidding ourselves or that we should kid ourselves that this exercise can succeed unless the industrialized countries are prepared to give something to the developing countries.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question and one supplementary question to the minister, if I may. I appreciate his answer to the Leader of the Opposition, that it was necessary to work out a common approach on commodity pricing with the other members of the north-south conference, particularly the developed members, but I would ask him whether that answer is in harmony with the urgency of Canada working out a position on commodity pricing to bring in at the UNCTAD-four conference in May of this year. We will not be able to wait the north-south conference has fully finished its deliberations since the UNCTAD-four conference has already been hailed the most significant of all international conferences at a special session of the United Nations. Developing nations are waiting to see what the developed nations are going to do about bargaining on commodity prices with regard to cocoa, copper, lead, zinc, tin, coffee, bauxite and the bulk of the other 18 primary commodities.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe Canada has already signed or has become a member of certain commodity agreements affecting certain commodities, but I would be happy to get further information on that question. UNCTAD-four is meeting in Nairobi, I believe, next month. It is part of the process involved in the north-south dialogue. My approach, really, is a simple one. The same problems are being tackled in a number of fora-a commonly-used term today-at UNCTAD-four, at the seventh special session and at GATT. The same reality is being examined and the same problems are being discussed. Probably UNCTAD-four will make some further progress,
International Economic Co-operation but I do not see these various meetings as being separate events. They are all part of the same ongoing effort to solve problems affecting the same reality, and the same reality is being examined at all these institutions.
I believe the most important one, the one the world will be watching most, is the north-south dialogue, because it is a unique exercise, one that is working in co-operation with the United Nations. Apart from the United Nations, it has a separate origin and a new format, and is expected to deliver results at the end of 1976. So they are all important and they are all working on the same problem. I do not see how any one of us could try to develop a separate, new or different policy for each of these conferences, when actually they are dealing with the same question in one aspect or another.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask more than one supplementary, but I will refrain from doing that as I expect it would lead to another debate. I want to move quickly to a question for the minister in respect of priorities respecting aid. As we know, continued aid is very much a part of the new economic order of events in the north-south structure. I would ask the minister about Canada's priorities for aid. If aid is to go to the least developed countries, how is it that a $25 million agreement has just been signed with Indonesia which is an oil producing and exporting country? How is it that we announced that agreement without any detail as to how that money is to be used in Indonesia?
I ask these questions because of the contrasting situation we have seen develop within the past 24 hours as a result of an earthquake in Guatemala, with 2,000 people dead and 5,000 injured, but I have yet to hear any announcement that Canada intends to provide emergency aid to Guatemala. I put this question in the context of the importance of Canadian people knowing who is to get the aid, and why it is going there.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the case of Guatemala, I have authorized CIDA today to make a special donation to the International Red Cross as a first step in what I hope will be a series of measures to assist the tragically-stricken population of Guatemala. We have made this grant through the International Red Cross and we are considering substantial contributions in the form of food aid. We are also considering a restructuring of our aid program in respect of Guatemala in order to meet their short-term emergency situation.
In the case of Indonesia, it is a very poor country, well within the ambit of the strategy. Even though its economy has been helped by oil revenues, it is still a country that is very poor and deserves our help.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Canadian position is very well laid out; that is, we have developed, very clearly, a five-year strategy for our development assistance. Also, I do not believe that Canada is going to go into a commission on a subject of this importance unless it has a position it proposes to advance. Is the government going to be asking for some type of agreement between the exporting and importing countries regarding an international price? Is the government going to be making some proposal for an agreement by which the exporting countries might reduce the price, in return for which the developing countries would give greater access to the markets of the developed countries or some reduction in the price of goods which they are shipping into those countries? It seems to me-

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext: Order, please. Having restricted one member earlier in respect of making a comment on the minister's statement as opposed to putting questions, I wonder if I might ask the honourable member to ask his question now.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was simply trying to make clear to the minister

what I had in mind. I am asking, what is the position which Canadian representatives will take on the energy commission in respect of the kind of policy that will be beneficial to Canada and at the same time beneficial to the other countries, particularly the exporting countries?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might state, in general terms, what I conceive to be the major objective that Canada will seek to achieve at the energy commission. The major objective, in our view, would be to develop arrangements that would make for long-term stability in the international energy market-or oil market, in so far as we are talking about oil-making it possible for a country like Canada and others in the world to make orderly plans within that framework over the long term.
Obviously, the question of price is an important one. The question of security of supply is an important one, as well. The question of indexation will be extremely important to the oil producers. One asks himself, as a participant in the commission, whether it would be desirable at this stage to get involved in these extremely difficult questions, thereby endangering at a very early stage the possibility of a fruitful dialogue. I believe it will be up to the co-chairmen of the commission on energy, the United States and Saudi Arabia, as well as the members of the commission, to work out the work program.
It would seem to me there will be an effort to establish a factual basis and to determine all the factors which are presently influencing the demand for energy in the world, as well as the supplies of energy, so that people can agree at least on the facts before they get into the very difficult policy questions of price, supply and indexation. I think these questions are among the main ones that will be dealt with. That, in general, is the best I can do in reply to the honourable member's question. We have been giving consideration to the membership on the energy commission, and we will be represented by senior officials on that commission and another official on the development commission, and we will have observers on the commission on raw materials and the commission on financial affairs.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to take too long, because I understand that due consideration must be given to the fact that fairly soon there will be a division on this amendment. I am pleased to see here in the chamber the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who will be able to support this amendment

because it relates to agriculture. He has become a friend of the agricultural producer and I am sure he would want to do everything to help production.
This is a very specific amendment for the producer of a specific product. In this case, it could well be purebred or exotic livestock. My colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) will take a few moments of the time of the House to make some remarks with regard to machinery.
The amendment is with regard to specialized production by a specialized corporation or individual, and to a specialized advertising agency and to specialized consumers. It is not a large area that we are covering. The necessity for this amendment is due to the fact that purebred livestock producers in one part of Canada, either western or eastern Canada, may be directing their advertising through a medium in the United States back to particular people in Canada. At present, it is left open to the interpretation of a government official as to whether that person can deduct the expense of advertising for income tax purposes. It would seem to me that, while this may be the manner in which the government would like to proceed, the provisions should be specific, and this is what the amendment would achieve.
I suggest the addition of the word "agricultural" to the amendment of the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy). I think this is a good amendment because it also deals with specifics. It is not a large business, but a specific one, and this is of fundamental importance. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) took exception to it the other day because he felt that it might cause an influx into Canada of foreign-owned magazines. But I would bring to his attention and to that of all those who want to oppose this legislation the fact that we have the Foreign Investment Review Act which protects the Canadian industry.
However, in certain areas we do not have adequate facilities within our borders with which to publicize our products, and that is why it is of fundamental importance for us to try to give sufficient assistance to producers to advertise their products adequately across this country to enable them to receive the highest price for their products, which is to the advantage of both the producers and the consumers, because that is what competition is all about.
Government statutes allow exemptions for catalogues and publications for the encouragement and promotional development of fine arts and religion. I see no reason why the motion of the hon. member for Timmins to include scientific or medical subjects should not be adopted, following which we would add agricultural products.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments in connection with motion No. 3. I believe motions Nos. 2 and 3 are being dealt with together. Unfortunately, I was not in the House yesterday afternoon when the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) spoke; I was in the resources committee. But I did have the opportunity of reading his remarks as recorded in Hansard. At the outset he said that this bill has taken a long time, about a year. This is true, but this is a very important piece of legislation as far as the people of Canada are concerned. It is a piece of legislation which possibly has brought in more correspondence than any other legislation which has been before the House since I came here in 1972. Consequently, it is important that we do take time with this bill.
The tenor of the correspondence which has come in, not only to myself but to other hon. members on both sides of this House, has been opposition to the bill. It is interesting to note that the Secretary of State throughout the year has remained adamant in his stand until the last day or two. Suddenly we were faced with a piece of correspondence or a news release from Reader's Digest to the effect that it is now in a position to comply with the bill or the regulations as to content.
In so far as this motion is concerned, the Secretary of State indicated in his speech yesterday that both motions Nos. 2 and 3 are very important, yet on the other hand he indicated he is not prepared to accept them. It seems to me that he is prepared to allow the interpretation of the regulations to be the guide, and the interpretation of the regulations in the past has been a movement back and forth depending on the whims and fancies of the Minister of National Revenue. It seems to me that it is important to companies doing business in Canada, and to individual
10672

citizens, to understand the law. The law should not be left to the interpretation, the whims and fancies of the minister or to the mandarins who administer the regulations or the legislation.
These two amendments set out specifically what the law is. They are amendments which anyone can understand. Often in recent years legislation was drafted in such a manner that it was almost impossible to understand, and it required interpretation. However, I am pleased to see that these two amendments leave no doubt as to what the publishing companies have to comply with. This is the way we should legislate in this country. Parliament is the sounding board; it is the legislative body which makes the law-and if we have a situation where things are done by regulation rather than by legislation, there is nothing but chaos. This is what has happened in the past year with this piece of legislation. If the minister had been specific and had left no doubt in the minds of the companies involved, we would have had a much shorter debate and arrived at a solution much earlier.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), when speaking yesterday, posed certain questions to the Secretary of State or to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen). The hon. member was concerned about what time-frame was allowed Reader's Digest in order for it to be within the law. Up until now that question has not been answered by the ministers involved or by any hon. member on the government side. However, certainly Reader's Digest at the moment is not in a position to comply with the ownership requirements or the shareholding requirements, and it seems to me that there must have been some arrangement made between Reader's Digest and the Department of National Revenue to allow it to continue publishing in Canada until such time as it complied with the specific regulations. If this is the case, I think it is only fair, and indeed it is incumbent upon the government, to advise this House what the time-frame is, because we certainly cannot make fish of one and fowl of the other. In other words, if Reader's Digest is to be allowed a certain time-frame during which it can comply with the regulations, then it is only fair that Time or any other magazine involved should be given similar consideration.
In closing, I must say I hope that at some time before we close the debate on these two amendments, or before we have a final vote on this bill, one or other of the ministers, or some hon. member on the government side, will stand and tell the House the true facts and what the time-frame is, in order that not only may Reader's Digest be in a position to carry on and comply, but perhaps in fairness Time magazine may be allowed to have a similar opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to participate in the debate and to make a few comments with regard to motions Nos. 2 and 3. In substance, the amendments deal with the aspect of "not substantially the same". Let me emphasize once more that along with a great many other members of parliament on all sides of the House, I was most surprised to learn that Reader's Digest had issued a press release the other day agreeing to the terms set out by the government. I am also

just as sure that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) was not in the least surprised. Some of us have endeavoured to get some information but have not been successful. It is my considered opinion that Reader's Digest was bludgeoned into this, or I could say it might have had a rubber hose used on it and in order to survive it issued the directive or press release. A good many of us are now wondering how Time magazine will react.
I will concede that the 75 per cent ownership and the other requirements as originally set out are in order, but let me repeat that, along with many of my colleagues and hon. members from the government side of the House, 80 per cent is an arbitrary and high amount of Canadian content and will, in my opinion, dilute the content of a magazine. It now looks as if we will have a czar of the magazine industry, which will result in a controlled press as far as magazines are concerned.
The minister, in his omnipotence, could step in and close down some magazines and let others operate. The president of Reader's Digest made the following statement some while back when appearing before the committee:
We cannot meet an 80 per cent substantially different content regulation. It would simply destroy the Digest basic publishing format. It would largely prevent us from republishing material from other publications to the extent that we would no longer be a digest of international articles. It is therefore our opinion that we would no longer have a publication that would be recognized by, or have the same or as much appeal, to our readers.
There has been an about-face in that I am aware that the minister has relented somewhat and will now allow digests of worldwide articles which may be used in the parent magazine but which cannot be the same and must be edited by the Canadian writer. I am assuming that this is a face-saving device because of the tremendous criticism that the government has received on the content issue which, let me repeat, is a form of censorship.
Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that Reader's Digest will not exist in fear and trembling at the whim of the Minister of National Revenue or his grand mandarins or the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), depending on who assumes control of this. A great many of us will be watching each issue. I know that a great many government officials will have their measuring sticks out, checking it like hawks.
I would also like to commend the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) for his amendment which requests special consideration for medical journals and scientific magazines, and also the subamendment of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) who is suggesting agricultural magazines be exempt and has presented a very good case for this type of magazine. I was delighted to see this was passed on division, but I am somewhat skeptical that when the votes come on motions Nos. 2 and 3, in all probability government members will change their view and vote against them.
As I mentioned earlier, the government has retreated on the Reader's Digest issue but only as a sop to the opposition. I am delighted to know that Reader's Digest is going to continue, even if in some restricted form. Let me also say, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), that I received more letters on the Reader's Digest subject and the possibility of its being discontinued as a
February 5, 1976

Canadian publication than on those two contentious issues of capital punishment and abortion. If anyone doubts that, they can come to my office and see the file of letters. This is an indication of how seriously a great many of the citizens of Canada, particularly those in my riding, view this matter. I received letters from other parts of the country than my own riding.
As the member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) pointed out the other day, the Secretary of State entertained representatives of Maclean-Hunter as witnesses before the committee examining this legislation and refused to allow a delegation from Reader's Digest to present their views on the subject. In addition, the hon. member pointed out that even some of the Liberal members of the committee were bumped because of their opposition to this bill. Surely that is not democracy.
Once this bill becomes law, the Secretary of State will be able to exercise his powers of censorship over other publications in Canada. This is a very potent weapon for the government to put in the hands of one of the henchmen of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I can see him now, lowering the boom on certain publications that expose the blunders and derogatory statements made by government officials and departments. This is the sort of club presently being used with such devastating effect by India's Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi.
There has been much criticism in the press. I assume most hon. members saw the article in this morning's Globe and Mail by Geoffrey Stevens which is a parody on Gilbert and Sullivan. He says that the Cullen rule is obnoxious on several grounds and, of course, the Minister of National Revenue has admitted that this Cullen rule is now the gospel of the government. I heard the minister on the CTV program "A.M." yesterday morning. Mr. Stevens wrote:
The "Cullen rule" was obnoxious on several grounds. It has no basis in law-and Mr. Cullen admitted as much when he said that, if the courts did not uphold his interpretation, the government would change the law.
That is a pretty strong statement, Mr. Speaker. He went on:
Unlike Bill C-58, the objective of the "Cullen rule" was simple discrimination-to force Time and Reader's Digest to abandon their Canadian editions, regardless of whether they met the Canadian citizenship requirements of C-58. And, given the realties of Canadian publishing, the "Cullen rule" meant that Canada would probably never have a magazine which reported fully to Canadians on events beyond our borders. An asinine rule.
The article concluded by saying:
What we have is not a "magazine policy". What we have is a thoroughly muddled government scrambling to save the political skins, if not the credibility, of two of its ministers.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

It was the Secretary of State who got the country and himself into this mess in the first place. speechtext:
Surely the Department of National Revenue, of all departments, ought never to be accused of arbitrariness and unfairness. Surely that department's reputation deserves protection. The implications of fair dealing extend beyond this bill. The Minister of National Revenue asks the House to give him carte blanche to determine the meaning of "substantially different" or "substantially the same" in connection with the publishing industry. At the moment he says that the pertinent figure is 80 per cent. Next week it may be another figure; it can change with the passage of time and from minister to minister as one minister succeeds another in that portfolio. The figure depends on the whim, the arbitrary decision of the government of the day. Let me quote what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said in this debate as reported on page 10586 of Hansard. He was speaking about the 80 per cent provision not being embodied in any statute. He said: 
It is also completely arbitrary in the sense that it can be changed whenever the minister changes his mind or whenever his cabinet colleagues change their minds. In that event there is to be no public discussion: there is to be a nice, cosy discussion within the confines of the minister's office or possibly in the cabinet room.
Surely we cannot accept any arbitrary interpretation of any part of a statute affecting the magazine and publishing industry of Canada. No fair-minded Canadian would accept this. Frankly, I regret the involvement of the Minister of National Revenue, for whom I have profound respect and indeed, affection. I would not expect the minister to act arbitrarily. Possibly he will be less arbitrary than others; but the principle remains. Who will be the minister tomorrow? I don't know. What confidence can we place in any minister of the day not to act arbitrarily? To what pressures will the minister be subjected? What pressure was brought to bear to permit this political face-saving involving only one magazine? Frankly, Mr. Speaker, that is all this is. The government's attempt to extricate itself from the mess it created by providing for the arbitrary exercise of ministerial discretion is unacceptable. We do not accept it; neither do those we represent accept it. I say this more in sadness than in anger.
Earlier I referred to Geoffrey Stevens' column in today's Globe and Mail. I shall quote part of the column in a minute, but before I do so let me emphasize that we did not disagree with the original concept and purpose of the bill. We were in favour of giving encouragement to the Canadian publishing industry. No one disagrees with that. Actually, I think most hon. members would unanimously support the idea. Unfortunately, the government's action has clouded the industry's horizon. I suggest, with all sincerity, that we shall all rue the day the government introduced the present measure unless we amend it as proposed. May I now read part of Mr. Geoffrey Stevens' column in this morning's Globe and Mail. He said:
Quite simply, we have in Ottawa a government that is so confused that it doesn't know what it is doing. We have a government which started out with a good idea-to protect the domestic Canadian magazine industry from unfair foreign competition. To this end, it introduced Bill C-58 which would require that, to be deemed Canadian for tax purposes, all magazines would have to be edited, controlled and at least 75 per cent owned in Canada. A sensible, long overdue step.
Mr. Stevens was writing about the peak of the affair. It has been all downhill ever since. We have stumbled from crisis to crisis, mistake to mistake, and come to the point at which deals are made-probably in the minister's office. Surely that is no way to encourage other Canadian magazines or Canadian writers. I am certain that magazines and writers of integrity do not normally indulge in back-room deals. I therefore urge the government to take time to think about this matter. Let us find an honourable way out of this completely unacceptable situation in which the Canadian magazine industry today finds itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure this afternoon of listening to a number of speeches on this amendment. They have raised a number of concerns in my mind. The most important thing that has been said has been the relative lack of answer by the government to the very important questions raised by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather). There has not only been a lack of answer with respect to the questions themselves, which certainly bear answer, but with respect to the nature of the questions. Aside from the specific answers, what the hon. member for Fundy-Royal was asking was the philosophy of this government in dealing with the rights of what, for want of a better term, might be called citizens in terms of the dangers that can occur as a result of discriminatory acts. The intervention that was brought to the attention of this House a day or so ago as the result of the statement by Reader's Digest was the most blatant evidence of lack of understanding of the importance of there being no discrimination in the operation of a government in the way in which rules and statutes are to be determined and administered.
This is a black day. When Bill C-58 came forward, I joined with others in not quarrelling with the general idea of the government to provide some equity and balance in terms of privilege. In a speech at that time, I suggested that we ought to consider the fairness of doing it in an arbitrary way. Sometimes the names create different attitudes toward the idea. For a publication or a group of publications, in this case two, to have a certain status in Canadian law, and they having committed themselves to the rules in existence at that time, it would be unfair suddenly to pull the rug out from under them. That is not the way things ought to be done and it is not the way that things are normally done in terms of taxation matters. If we were dealing with anything but an American edition, Canadians would rise up and cry "Foul". I cry "Foul" regardless of what publication. I would also cry "Foul" if we were talking about something else, because this is not the way things ought to be done.
The first blunder of the government, therefore, was not the intent but the method it adopted. Having unfairly dealt with two publications, we heard the other day that there is a second discrimination. Some call it a deal, a back-room arrangement, or put some other label on it. I am not privy to the reasons for the discrimination; I can only guess. However, one publication is being dealt with differently from the other. I take no comfort in the fact that Reader's Digest, a magazine I enjoy and about which I have received a lot of correspondence from my constituents, is being favoured by this discriminatory back-door arrangement. In my respectful submission, it is a dreadful arrangement that this government has made.
Although this action may appear to benefit one particular magazine, in the long run the government may have opened the door to justice and equity. It will depend on who is the minister, his attitude, his relationship with his colleagues, his clout and, to quote an adage from ancient times in British justice, how long is the chancellor's foot? It is as simple as that. If that is the way the law is to be administered in Canada, with arrangements made, issues settled and rights determined in the cabinet room or in the
Adjournment Motion
office of the Minister of National Revenue, whether this or some future minister, or some other minister, I say that is wrong. I hope there are sufficient people on all sides of this House who feel strongly about this. Regardless of the transitory embarrassment this may be to the minister, I hope they will stand up and say it is wrong. I hope that happens because this is a very important principle.
What has happened in Canada is that we rely more and more on the administrative tribunal. We have moved away from the courts, whether we are talking about public service legislation, as we talked about in the Finkelman committee this morning, or transportation. We are moving to where the decisions of government are being made by commissions. That is not a happy trend in a free society. Commissions and boards can act as lightning-rods to take the heat off governments. The responsibility is basically a political one in terms of decisions that ought to be made. However, even if that is a bad trend, and even if the administrative tribunal is bad, before the administrative tribunal-

Contract of Employment

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE INFORMATION TO PUBLIC ON CONTRACTS OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-267, respecting employment with the Government of Canada not covered by the Public Service Employment Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is a simple one. It is to provide information to the public as to all contracts of employment entered into by the office of the Prime Minister or by government departments. What I am proposing is an amendment which would add to the Public Service Employment Act a clause which would require the publishing, in full, each month in the Canada Gazette of every contract of employment not covered by the Public Service Employment Act to which the government of Canada is a party, where a person is contractually engaged by a department of the government or by the office of the Prime Minister.
We ought, all of us, to be concerned about the sharp increases which have taken place in recent years in government expenditure and the very large increases which have taken place in the number of civil servants. I am a member of a party which believes that, as life becomes more complex, government must assume greater responsibility than in the past for meeting the needs of the people. I do not, therefore, object to increases in the number of public servants. However, I join with many people who are concerned about the very large increases which have taken place in the number of public servants, particularly the tremendous increase which has taken place in recent years in expenditure for the hiring of consultants who work for the government and are paid by the people of Canada, through their taxes, but who are hired with none of the safeguards which are enumerated in the Public Service Employment Act.
Let me illustrate what I mean by quoting from the Globe and Mail of March 17, 1975, a couple of paragraphs from a news report which appeared in that issue:
Government spending for "Professional and Special Services" will reach at least $982.5 million this year (1975-76) according to initial government estimates and will almost certainly be higher after supplementary estimates are introduced throughout the year.
The figure represents an increase of 18.3 per cent over spending on consultants in the current fiscal year and a 35.9 per cent increase since 1973-74.
During the same two-year period the overall government work force ... has risen by about 10 per cent to about 255,000 from 231,000.
That is the picture of what is happening. There has been a steady increase, one with which I do not entirely disagree, in the number of public servants in recent years. But look at what has happened in the senior positions, in the executive positions which are classified as SX positions. On October 1, 1974, I put a question on the order paper as follows:
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner (London East)).]
What was the increase in the number of senior officers, SX-1, SX-2, SX-3, SX-4, for each year from 1968 to 1973, or, in the case of new departments, etc., from their inception to 1973?
The answer was as follows, and I am sure the figures are out of date by now:
The increase in the number of senior SX officers for each year from 1968 to 1973 for all departments and agencies of the public service was as follows: in 1968 there were 381 senior SX officers. This total rose to 412 in 1969, 535 in 1970, 602 in 1971, 720 in 1972 and 895 in 1973.
So there were almost 2'/2 times as many in 1973 as there were five years earlier. The people of Canada have a right to ask whether such an increase was necessary. In 1975 I asked a question which was answered on March 17 of that year. The answer can be found in Hansard of that day. I asked:
What categories and ranks specifically of public servants other than SX are considered part of the senior management complement of government departments?
The answer came down-I shall not read the list department by department-showing there were over 450 of these positions. Then on January 28, 1975, I asked the question:
How many people in the public service, excluding those in the SX salary range, are earning salaries equivalent to or more than $25,500, which is the minimum SX-1 salary?
The answer was as follows:
As of September 30, 1974, 3,307 public servants, including those in levels deemed to be equivalent to senior executive officer levels, earned salaries equivalent to or more than $25,500 per annum.
Mr. Speaker, despite this tremendous increase in employees in the senior levels of the public service, details of which I have placed on record, we spent, in 1975, close to $1 billion on consultants hired by contract. And, as I pointed out, none of the restraints or detailed information which are expected by the public and required by the Public Service Employment Act are applicable in these circumstances.
Back in 1974 I asked how many employees in each department were employed on a term basis, a casual basis or a contract basis. The answer was voluminous. I am not the only hon. member who has asked questions on this subject. I tried to count the number of those who make more than $20,000 a year on contract. My arithmetic may not be exact, but I do not think it is far wrong. In the Department of Communications there are 15; in the Department of Consumer Affairs, two; in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, four; in Indian Affairs and Northern Development, five; Justice, 10; Manpower, three; Regional Economic Expansion, six; Science and Technology, five. I could go on and on.
On October 1, 1974, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) asked how many consultants were engaged by each of the departments as of that date. Again, there was a long answer and I do not have time to read it all into the record. But let me give the House a few illustrations. In the Department of External Affairs an editorial consultant was employed for two years, for which he received $52,800. There was paid the sum of $40,000 in connection with specialized projects in the field of international law.
Take the Treasury Board, the people who are supposed to monitor the whole system, the people who are supposed to protect us from overspending. Here we find a contract to advise on questions pertaining to federal public service
February 5, 1976

compensation programs. The consultant worked, as far as I can tell, for six months and was granted $33,000. Another consultant was called in to advise on matters pertaining to federal decentralization. He, it seems, worked for three months and received $18,000. Another was engaged to advise on operations research. He worked for a year and received $23,000. Another man worked to advise the secretary of the Treasury Board on the form of the accounts of Canada and other areas of financial management; he seemed to work for about six months and received $25,000. A company was engaged to analyse the role and long-range purpose of the personnel policy branch; they worked for about five months and were paid $36,000. Another man worked to advise and assist the Treasury Board secretariat on administrative procedures regarding personnel management; he seemed to work for about six months and received $46,000. I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker.
Not so long ago I discussed this whole question of the number of senior public servants and consultants being engaged, the fees they were charging and getting. One man told me-I am not going to reveal his name because I did not say I would, but he has been in the senior levels of government, both federal and provincial, for many years and I consider him to be one of the best public servants this country has ever had-that the system is out of control. Those were his exact words. He said no one is looking at these things any more.
A large sum of money is involved here; the last year for which figures are available showed an expenditure of almost $1 billion. Whether the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) will succeed in holding the line this year-a year of supposed restraint-to the figure last year, I do not know. In answer to a question I asked him when he first announced his program, he said that the budget was frozen and would not increase.
Let me cast my mind back to the last time the Government of Canada, this present Liberal government, during the period 1971-72, said it would freeze for one year the number of civil servants. They did it, Mr. Speaker, but during that period of time the number of consultants hired and the consequent amount spent increased dramatically by the standards of that year, though much less than today or even last year. But based on my experience here, I have the feeling that this year will be no different, that there will be further increases in the number of consultants hired and the amount of money paid to them.
I want the Government of Canada to be efficient. I want it to hire the best people it can to do the jobs that need to be done. But I find it very difficult to be enthusiastic-I am putting it mildly-about participating in any program that says to people down at the bottom, both in the public service and in private industry, "We are determined that inflation must be checked, that we must stop inflation, and therefore we have passed legislation under which your increase in wages or salaries cannot be more than 10 per cent this year, 8 per cent next year and 6 per cent the following year".
Not that that plan will not work, Mr. Speaker, but I find it difficult to support such a program when I see how generous-I could use stronger language and say profli-
Contract of Employment
gate-this government has been in its treatment of senior civil servants. I see their expenses and salaries increasing, as are their trips both inside and outside the country. There has been a tremendous increase in recent years in the number of consultants hired by virtually every department of government.
My proposal is a very simple one. I am not saying that contracts to consultants must cease. Neither am I saying that at this point in time the amount of money spent or the number of consultants hired should be reduced. I am simply saying to this government, and to any government that may be in office in future years, that it makes sense to me that we let the people of Canada know as much as possible about what the government is doing, and that therefore each month there should be an announcement in the Canada Gazette of the contracts that have been let, the number of people hired as consultants, what they are to do and how much they are to be paid.
One member on the government side will shortly get up and tell us that there are hundreds of thousands of people who are hired for a week or a month, many of them to undertake very ordinary jobs at somewhere between the minimum wage of $3.50 an hour, or whatever it is at the moment, and $5 an hour. I realize it would not be very productive to list every single one. I also realize that if my proposal were enacted in the precise terms written into the bill there would be problems. If any member on the government side wants to amend the bill to provide that only contracts that pay more than $20,000 a year and up should be reported in the Gazette, then I would be very happy to accept that amendment.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the bill I am introducing is a simple one. It is not aimed at the government. It is asking for the publication of information that the people of Canada are entitled to have, and I urge hon. members to support passage of this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE INFORMATION TO PUBLIC ON CONTRACTS OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss Bill C-267 in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) in its present form from the point of view of the increased cost to the taxpayer that would be involved should the bill become law. The proposal apparently includes contracts with both companies and individuals. As the House is no doubt aware, a company is a legal person; therefore, we may interpret the hon. member's suggestion as meaning both personal service contracts and third party contracts.
It is difficult to place a numerical value on the numbers of contracts in the public service, excluding Crown corporations. However, considering major users we would estimate it to be in the area of 6,000. It is likely that that figure is a minimum one as all departments, the Treasury Board secretariat and Supply and Services have authority to issue contracts, either personal service or otherwise. These would include everything from cleaning services to engineer to personnel consulting to foreign aid to small post offices in rural areas as well as urban areas. The publishing of all such contracts on a monthly, or indeed on any basis, is ludicrous. Publishing costs would be astronomical, to say nothing of the number of additional pages needed in the Canada Gazette.
