The Canadian International Development Agency lets approximately 1,000 contracts for foreign aid services as well as internal services. These contracts contain all specifications for work to be accomplished as well as compensation both in the form of salary and allowances. At a minimum of two pages per contract, it is estimated that with translation one contract could be published per page of the Gazette. This means that, using both sides of one page in the Gazette, two contracts could be published. From this point, simple arithmetic tells us that for CIDA alone the Gazette, in terms of contract publication, would use 500 pages.
The situation regarding personal service contracts, that is, contracts with individuals, is almost as bad. Consider the Post Office with its hundreds of contracts to individuals as postmasters in rural areas. Even taking a minimum of 1,000, we find ourselves with a 500-page Gazette. We would estimate that there are some 2,500 personal service contracts let in the public service; therefore, again simple arithmetic gives us a Gazette of 1,250 pages for contracts alone.
As I mentioned, we have no way of knowing specifically how many contracts are let in the public service during the course of one year, but just from conservative figures one can see the utter folly of demanding publication of each every month as is suggested by the hon. member.
In terms of cost of publication, let us consider that the Gazette averages approximately 20 pages at an annual subscription rate of $25. At 250 pages, these subscription costs could rise to 12.5 the present rate, bringing the yearly rate to approximately $312. Somehow, I do not think we would get any subscribers. Also, let us consider translation costs which could be necessarily the responsibility of individual departments. At present, if we contract with an individual or company who deals in the French language, the contract is drawn up in French. The same applies to the English language, so there is little problem in individual departments. However, to publish these contracts we must have all of them available in both official languages. In order to accommodate this work load, we must hire more translators or, of course, we could contract at five-cents per word.
A conservative estimate gives us an average of approximately $50 per contract. Multiplying this by our estimate of 6,000 contracts gives us an approximate cost of $300,000 initially. We cannot say what the total cost may amount to as contracts expire at any interval during the year and new ones are let, and for every new one a translation must be made. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has brought forward a very interesting proposal. What was the most interesting part of the debate so far was the unusual suggestion by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) when he said he intended to vote against the bill. This left a little hope in my heart, as I thought perhaps history was to be made tonight and we would actually have the opportunity to vote on a private member's bill. I do not know whether those words were in the hon. member's notes, whether that was a slip, or whether he was indicating he agrees with me that we ought to have greater opportunity to vote on private members' bills rather than merely set them aside.
I read this short bill with great interest. It appeared that the intention of the hon. member is to answer what has been a cry of many people, in terms of big government and complex governmental matters. His intention appears to be an answer to the public's right to know. What has taken place in respect of our order paper and a number of other things in this place would indicate that the right of the public and of members of parliament to know what is going on is diminishing at about the same rate as the complexity of government and government intervention is increasing. The introduction of the computer and sophisticated methods of communication have not really helped the situation.
In looking at the bill presented by the hon. member, it says two things: it says that the public has a right to know, and governments have a duty to disclose. The hon. member, hopefully, would have the bill go to the committee where the objections of hon. members, such as the one by the hon. member for Wellington, which could be entitled "It cannot be done", could be considered.
Let me say to the hon. member for Wellington that I am as conscious as he is of cost, but I would hope that the principle and the main thrust of this proposal could be sent to the committee for examination. It could be considered there, and it may be that the committee would not accede to the request of the hon. member for Winnipeg North. What he suggests, I admit, would result in monumental costs of preparation. It could be that these contracts could be filed at a central registry where they would be available to those interested.
The principle which has been set forth in this bill having regard to the matter of disclosure ought not to be rejected. I regret that the hon. member for Wellington would vote against the matter if he has the chance, having particular regard to the principle being put forward. There are very few people in Canada, even in the cabinet, who are fully cognizant of what is happening in all departments, or even the department of one's seatmate. The organization of the business of government is becoming more difficult and more complex. I do not believe that on every occasion a government does not disclose something it does it wilfully. I do not believe there is any feeling in the public service that they are going to make mistakes which will not be disclosed. Alll I am saying is that our procedures have come to the point where it is easy for them not to disclose. Rather than having a little trouble with it at the outset, they will just not give out the information. I think it is important that we, as representatives of the people, have
February 5, 1976

access to that information and that people who are interested in particular areas have access to it.
I do not often support an NDP bill or a proposition advanced by a member of the NDP, but I think this is a sound one and I hope the government, and the members here today, who actually have the decision as to whether or not they will let it go, not the government, will give careful consideration to the principle of the bill.
Let us deal with the question of consultant contracts. There is a suspicion in the land-from time to time there are enough pieces of evidence which tend to confirm that suspicion-that the consultant contracts in the public relations field are one of the largest patronage operations available to government. I hope that is not so, but that is the suspicion.
I raised the matter with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) in the House with respect to the Price Rubin contract. That matter has never been satisfactorily answered in terms of the time when Treasury Board approval was given in relation to the payment out of moneys under that contract. It is an established fact that one of the members of that organization at one time was a partner of the Minister of Labour. I am not suggesting that that by itself indicates that the Minister of Labour had his finger in the giving of the contract, but what I am suggesting is that that relationship gave the appearance of that, and that is very bad for our system. It was a bad thing for the Minister of Labour. He wrote me about it, he felt sensitive about it. He would not have felt sensitive about it if there was not a bad appearance, an unusual appearance.
I recognize that we cannot tender for every contract; it is impossible; the cost would be impossible. But if we cannot tender for them all I do not think it is unreasonable that we should at least disclose them all. I hope there is no member who would disagree with me. When we talk about consultant contracts we are talking about a substantial amount of government moneys. If my recollection of the current estimates is correct, we are talking about $900 million in consultant contracts, a tremendous increase over the previous fiscal year. Some of that could be attributed to the fact that government activities have expanded, but I believe that some of it-and this is important to me as a member in the national capital area who represents a large part of the public service-is due to the fact that the public service of our country, far from being too large and far from growing too rapidly, is in fact under-challenged in terms of its ability to do a job.
I have raised this matter before in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates when the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) was before the committee. I spoke about the practice of turning to consultants whenever there is a little problem within a department or a small study to be made.
In fact the public service of this country is under-challenged. When that happens the public service becomes the butt of everyone who would say that bigness is bad, government is growing and is too large, and civil servants sit around and do not do any work. I have been in a lot of government offices and have found that in some cases that is true, but I have also been in the offices of Dupont of
Contract of Employment
Canada, the offices of General Motors and many big private enterprise organizations, and I see the water cooler crowd there too. That happens to be one of the difficulties with respect to business. So, whether the criticism comes from any particular area of this House or not, 1 do not accept the contention that the public service is necessarily too large and that that is the major criticism with respect to the public service.
I believe that the public service is under-challenged in terms of the ability of the men and women in the public service to handle the problems they have. This is something at which we will have to look. I think we have been somewhat unfair with the public service in many ways because every time a government gets into trouble it pounces on the public service as being necessarily too large, instead of looking at the priorization of the programs of government to see whether, not the public service but the governors of the country have their priorities set in such a way that large parts of these programs go on and on without being considered in terms of their relevance. They take on lives of their own.
What happens is that either a government freezes or, on the other hand, it appoints a commission, a one shot operation, to examine the operations of the government. It will come moving in, and instead of this examination being something that would be welcomed generally by the public servants who want to advance in their careers, like everyone else who wants to have a reasonable security of tenure in a challenging job, they feel themselves to be the target of these periodic examinations that go on whenever a government is in trouble.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North is in order. I think the growth factor is out of control in many ways and we do a disservice to the public servant and to the public service generally in allowing that to happen. Perhaps we ought to consider a mechanism such as a continuing commission on government operations and management, recognizing that it is large but recognizing at the same time that, as a result of the attitudes of government and the necessities of society opportunities in the public service were opened up but that they should not be expanded like a balloon and then knocked down. It is most unfair for the people in the public service. It should be a kind of continuing operation.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned the level of compensation in the public service. In the higher levels of the public service of this country, the deputy ministers and assistant deputy ministers, we have in fact the highest paid public servants, dollar for dollar, and comparing dollars to pounds sterling or francs, compared with any public servants in the world.

I suspect that the minister has a mandate to decentralize. What will he do? I would bet that this will be borne out by the facts: he will ask all his officials what departments could be moved. That is not establishing a criterion. That is taking the administrative point of view, because there is no examination of what might happen if an area of undertaking within a department, a branch of a department, or indeed of a whole department is moved out, in terms of its function and as to whether that movement may do nothing more than create another element of bureaucracy.
I suspect that what is happening with respect to the government's program is that it is considering decentralization from two points of view, the first being the creation of the presence of the government, and therefore employment and benefits, in certain areas of Canada, and secondly, reading the secret cabinet documents I released on September 3, 1975, it is tied into the whole program concerned with units working in French, none of which has to do with the efficient operation of the public service of Canada.

I do not want to occupy too much time of the House with respect to this matter, but obviously I feel very strongly about it. subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before private members' hour I was discussing the dreadfully difficult situation which has arisen from the government's action in connection with this bill. The difficulty has little to do with the bill itself, as the bill seeks to establish a principle on which there is no significant division of opinion either in the country or in the House, namely, that there ought not to be any special privilege for magazines which operate, in the main, offshore, so to speak, but which also print editions for this country.
The difficulty which has been alluded to on second reading, and now, during report stage, has been compounded by the government's imposing on the magazine policy of Canada a discriminatory aspect which ought not to exist in any Canadian law expressed in the form of statute or regulations. In the present instance the sin is greater and more reprehensible because the government proposes to enact regulations by ministerial edict.
Before the dinner adjournment I suggested what we, of this House, feel about the place of government, about parliamentary responsibilities, and about the duties of people in politics. I suggested that we look on administrative tribunals as a sort of second level of governmental structure which operates independently of the political structure of government and is not responsive to the political process in a free society. The particular statute we are discussing would create a tribunal, under the aegis of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen), which cannot even be graced with the appellation "administrative." Here we have discrimination at its worst.
First the government changed the rules which, to begin with, have been shown to be patently unfair. What was done ought not to have been done, particularly if one

considers the commitment to an important industry with regard to the existence of certain rules. But it has gone one step further. Having changed the rules, the government has decided that magazines coming from offshore, or other countries, fall into two categories, two classes. They say, that Reader's Digest should be given special treatment; as for the treatment of Time magazine, it is nothing but unfairness compounded by unfairness, inequity by inequity and, I suggest, stupidity. Is it any wonder the people of Canada have their doubts about the government? Is it any wonder, as Mr. Geoffrey Stevens said in this morning's Globe and Mail, people think that in Ottawa we have a government so confused it does not know what it is doing?

I appreciate that. I admire them. I encourage them as well. They are joining a growing mass of Canadians who are looking at this legislation that is applied without benefit of legitimacy in terms of anything written. Rather, it is applied in terms of justice that could vary with the length of a chancellor's foot, and even vary with the chancellor or the disposition of the minister or the government, or the influence of that minister or the government. That kind of variation makes it a mockery in terms of those principles that ought to govern the life of this country. As I said at the beginning, I have no hesitation in saying that I admire anyone who is prepared to stand against that kind of application.
Mr. Geoffrey Stevens, in a column in this morning's Globe and Mail on the "Cullen rule" wrote, and I quote:
The "Cullen rule" was obnoxious on several grounds. It had no basis in law (and Mr. Cullen admitted as much when he said that, if the courts did not uphold his interpretation, the government would change the law).

speechtext:
I suppose I can in some way justify myself to my colleagues by saying that I, as a person, refuse to disown my own principles for my own personal benefit and certainly cannot be expected to do so for someone else's. I have great respect for these men and I have a great respect for the opinions which have been presented on behalf of the government and by those who support the bill. I can only hope that those on the other side of the issue will have an equal amount of respect for those who differ with them. There is in this instance a genuine disagreement as to what is the best thing to do in the Canadian publishing field.
I am sure my feelings are shared by all members of the House of Commons when I say I strongly support the stated intention of this bill, that is, to assist the Canadian publishing industry. The question is: does the bill before us achieve that objective, or are there better ways in which this could be done? I think there are.
Because of the importance of the bill and the fact that it is a government measure, in the early days of Bill C-58 I took extraordinary steps to try to become acquainted with all sides of the question. I telephoned and wrote to all those directly affected, including Macleans, Time, Reader's Digest, MD of Canada and Modern Medicine asking them to present their views to me so that I might be able to make an informed judgment. I also discussed the matter with members of the government and with my colleagues in my own caucus. I did so to feel satisfied in my own mind that the decision I was about to arrive at was, indeed, the right one. I am satisfied I have now been exposed to all aspects of the subject.
I might also say that I am not an advocate of Time, Reader's Digest, or of the other magazines affected. I am certainly not a computer printout in favour of any of those publications. I am taking the position I am taking today because I believe it is the right one. I cannot accept the premise that this bill will in fact assist Canadian publishers in the way it should.
The crux of the difficulties in which the Canadian periodical industry finds itself is, in fact, a shortage of advertising revenue sufficient to generate a truly healthy publications industry. In addition, I believe there is a real concern about the effects of unfair competition resulting from the dumping of editorial matter into Canada. These concerns are real and genuine and they should be dealt with by the House in a substantive way.
I notice that the Senate Committee on the Mass Media indicated that there were really two basic problems encountered by the publishing industry. The first was the volume of overflow magazines coming into Canada primarily from the United States. The second was the intense competition in Canada among the various sectors of the media for the advertising dollar. Does the bill before us address itself to either of these central questions? I say it does not.
First, in connection with overflow magazines coming into Canada from the United States, the bill we are discussing does not even deal with the question at all though 
it is a substantial problem. For example, in 1964, a year for which I have the statistics, the number of overflow magazines coming in from the U.S. came close to 182,000,000. Saids of domestic magazines, excluding Time and Reader's Digest, totalled 418,000,000. This means that roughly half the magazines which are sold in Canada are in fact produced in the U.S.A. and sold in this country. This may well be a major problem but I have not seen anything in bill C-58 which deals with it or even pretends to do so.
The other substantial question with respect to this issue relates to an entirely different aspect, that is, the amount of advertising money spent in Canada by advertisers which in fact finds its way into the pockets of producers of Canadian magazines. Yesterday, or the day before, speaking on one of the amendments before us I indicated-and I was speaking off the top of my head-that the statistic was 2.8 per cent-that 2.8 per cent of the advertising dollar went into the pockets of the periodical industry in Canada. I have subsequently learned that this figure was not quite accurate. The fact is, it is 2.3 per cent. That is the last figure I have, for the year 1974. In the United States 6.5 per cent of the advertising dollar is spent in the periodical industry. In the United Kingdom it is 8.5 per cent, in France 16.8 per cent, in West Germany 27.9 per cent, and in Italy 33.2 per cent.
The real competitors of the magazine industry in this country are radio, television and newspapers. For instance, newspapers in this country corner 28.6 per cent of the advertising dollar spent in Canada. Television accounts for 14.1 per cent, radio for 11 per cent, business publications 2.9 per cent, and supplements 1.6 per cent. And, as I have said in Canada the periodical industry, to which we are addressing ourselves, gets 2.3 per cent.
It would be interesting to quote from the Senate committee report on the media in this connection. "Most magazine publishers in Canada do not regard the overflow circulation as a primary problem for them. It is simply part of their environment. What they are aware of, though, is the intense competition for advertising revenues between themselves and other sectors of the media. It is a scramble between radio, television, newspapers and magazines for available advertising dollars and the attention of audiences."
Between 1954 and 1968 the magazines' share of total advertising revenues dropped from 4.2 per cent to 2.3 per cent. The bill we are considering does not deal with that question at all. We can see a trend on the graph militating against the publishing industry in this country because of its inability to get a sufficient percentage of the advertising revenue available in Canada. That is a matter the bill fails to deal with at all.
The solution is to increase the amount of advertising from the 2.3 per cent level to a much more significant level, one which would create in Canada a healthy magazine industry.
Diversion of revenue could easily be achieved in the Income Tax Act by declining to allow tax exemptions for advertising unless a minimum of 5 per cent of such advertising were directed to the periodical industry. I would think that a ceiling should be placed on this; to be reasonable, one would not look at those figures in relation to advertisers spending less than $100,000 a year. But if they
February 5, 1976

spent more than that, surely it would be proper for us to say they must allocate a certain proportion to periodicals. Surely it would be appropriate for us to say that they must divert a certain proportion of that advertising into the magazine industry if we want to pay more than lip service to the industry and, indeed, make it a healthy and prosperous segment of our economy. This would be beneficial to those in the field, the writers and all the multiplicity of people who are involved, and I think it would be a giant step toward creating some kind of cultural identity in Canada through the printed word in magazines.
Let me review for a moment what advertising revenue would be diverted from the four magazines that are primarily affected by this piece of legislation. As for Reader's Digest, in light of the recent announcement of its ability to comply with the legislation, obviously there will be no diversion of revenue from Reader's Digest to some other periodical in Canada. So from that standpoint there will be nil benefit to other publishers in Canada so far as Reader's Digest is concerned.
With respect to Modern Medicine and MD of Canada I do not want to go through the arguments all over again. I simply indicate that, in my humble view, there will be no diversion of advertising revenue either. The first point to be made in this respect is that these two magazines are free distribution magazines. They do contain Canadian advertisements now, but where would those advertisements go if in fact the two magazines cease publishing in Canada? Would they go to Maclean's magazine or to Weekend supplements? Anyone who knows anything about advertising knows that that advertising can only go into another trade magazine directed to that exclusive market.
Those who advertise medical products are not going to advertise their products to a group of farmers or to a group of people in the industrial field. They will try to direct their advertising to where it will pay the biggest dividends, which would be in the medical field. To my knowledge there is not one substantive magazine that will pick up that advertising revenue.
There may be some who might argue, as the Secretary of State argued, that in fact these magazines and others will still be available on the newsstands anyway, so there is no problem in regard, for instance, to access to or availability of information for Canadian doctors or others. I simply point out a self-evident feature: those two magazines have never been sold on a Canadian newsstand to date, and I can see no reason for believing they ever will in the future, because they do not have a dollar tag attached to them. So I suggest that argument does not mean much in terms of availability of information to Canadian doctors. I cannot see any likelihood of anyone continuing to publish either of these medical journals in Canada in the future when in fact they do not sell them. They are free circulation magazines.
In respect to Time magazine, what diversion of advertising dollars will there be to the Canadian periodical industry? This is a much more difficult case about which to make a substantive point. In my view, as a result of my studies of the question, I have concluded that there will be very little. I base my conclusion in part on this observa-
Non-Canadian Publications
tion, that in Time Canada a large percentage of advertising consists of multinational ads, such as Haig & Haig, General Motors or whatever. These corporations also advertise in the United States. According to admissions made by the government, Time magazine will still be available in Canada; therefore Canadians will be exposed to the same advertising to a very substantial extent, the difference being that it was bought and paid for in the United States. It comes into Canada and we achieve no benefits from it whatsoever. So I do not really see that there is that much diversion of advertising.
There is another point in this regard. Advertisements which appear in Time magazine also have duplicates in many instances within the Canadian magazine. Exactly the same advertisement is placed in two different magazines, not an unusual practice for advertisers. Is it really reasonable to presume that if Time is not longer published in Canada they will place two identical ads in Maclean's magazine or some other Canadian publication? It is highly unlikely, in my view. In fact I think it is absurd to imagine this would happen.
I have therefore concluded that in terms of diversion of advertising dollars to the magazine industry this bill is just not what its advocates have said it is. In addition, there is the argument whether any diversion that might take place would go into the periodical industry or into some other media, such as radio or television. Clearly in this respect one has no more reason to believe it will all be diverted into the publications field as opposed to arguing that it will be diverted into other forms of media.
I have therefore concluded that the best answer to the problem of genuinely assisting the magazine industry is a reallocation of Canadian advertising, bringing a minimum portion of it to the Canadian periodical industry. I would suggest 5 per cent might be a base from which to start.
Let me next consider the competition aspects of the proposed legislation now before us. There was one very legitimate argument that causes us all some concern, I think, and that is the editorial dumping of material into Canada at rates not compensatory with the cost of generating that editorial material. Indeed that could bring about unfair competition for the Canadian magazine industry. However, does this bill really solve the problem? I do not think it does at all. Although it deals with it in part, we already have legislation on our books directed toward dumping and it would seem to me appropriate that the dumping question ought to be dealt with in dumping legislation.
The next point I am concerned about is the elimination or minimization of competition to Maclean's and other Canadian magazines by the removal of other magazines from Canada. Competition is something we all pay lip service to, some of us more genuinely than others. I think we would all agree that competition run rampant is not necessarily a good think and that we must protect our Canadian industries. None the less should we protect them in such a way as to preserve for some in the Canadian magazine industry a virtual monopoly? I do not think this would be in the interests of the Canadian public.
In response to the statement of the Secretary of State in regard to Canadian magazines, let me say that even the magazines that might have to go back to the United States

February 5, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
will still be available in Canada. There is no question that that is largely true. In the case of the two medical journals I would disagree, so this argument really does not cut that much ice with me.
The fact is that Time magazine will indeed be available in Canada. The difference will be that there will be no Canadian ownership of Time, no Canadian control of Time, no Canadian content in Time, and no Canadian jobs generated as a result of its sale in Canada. In terms of the global national interest, I think those negative factors ought to be taken into account.
Let me look for a moment at the nationalism question. Have the Canadian people been stampeded into supporting a proposition that effectively makes nationalism a vehicle for wiping out legitimate competition and for lining the pockets of the publishing elite in Canada? I think there is reason for believing that may well be the case. I am nervous about that possibility and think it is inappropriate for a government to contribute in any way to that sort of thing happening. I am not saying it is a certainty, I am saying that I am nervous that this in fact will be the case, and I am not proposing to support the bill for this and a lot of other reasons.
There has been a lot of talk about this nationalism question. I am inclined to think that some would believe this under the guise of nationalism, and I think we are all economic, cultural nationalists in one way or another, and I certainly am. I am not prepared under that banner to come to the conclusion that we must have one set of standards for that which is Canadian and another set altogether which denies fair and equal treatment simply by virtue of the fact that it happens to be a foreign operation with which we are dealing. Indeed we have to protect our industries. I do not care if we nationalize them in many instances, but I do not want to see us simply rejecting or ejecting them from Canada by unfair and inappropriate treatment.
Let us look at the larger question that has been spoken about a great deal in this House, and that is the question of government control over editorial content. I must admit that in principle I have no objection to the government being involved in content regulations. In practice it is an extremely difficult area to be involved in, and I think there are considerable difficulties and dangers. However, I am not one who believes that the CRTC regulations, for instance, respecting Canadian content are bad. Clearly we have to take steps from time to time to encourage our own Canadian artists, writers and so on. I have no objection to these content regulations in principle, but I want to look at them very carefully to ensure that they achieve the objective we have in mind.
If we were to judge the newspaper industry in Canada in the same way we propose to judge the periodical industry in Canada with an "80 per cent not substantially the same as" rule. I am of the opinion on the basis of my research that there would hardly be a newspaper in Canada which would be allowed to publish. I do not know of any, including the Toronto Star, the Globe and Mail and others, which really could conform to an "80 per cent substantially dif-

ferent" from that which has ever appeared anywhere else rule.
That might be over-stating the case, but the principle is substantially right. We have established one set of rules for a particular publication industry, and have completely ignored those rules in respect of another larger segment. Perhaps there might be some good reason, and we might find if we ever debate it that in respect of the newspaper business there is no government with sufficient political influence to resist the onslaught to which it would be subjected. Politically we could not afford to do this in that industry, and I am not too sure we ought to have a different set of rules in respect of this industry.
This amendment I have put forward defines a Canadian periodical, and I want to deal with my definition of it. Before going into that I want to make a point in respect of the bill the government has put forward, C-58. This bill also defines a Canadian periodical, but not so much through the legislation we have before us but in fact through an interpretation of that legislation which is not before us. This is a difficult thing to accept, and I will deal with that more specifically later.
Effectively my approach to this is to bring within the law before parliament the definition of what a Canadian periodical is so that all of us can debate it and decide whether we agree. My definition parallels to some extent the definition already contained within the law: 75 per cent of the directors of the said firm must be Canadians; 75 per cent of its ownership must be in the hands of Canadians; its editing and publishing function must be controlled in Canada; all of its publication function must be conducted in Canada by Canadians; and not more than 40 per cent of its content can be first published in a single periodical outside Canada.
Effectively the difference is this: the 80 per cent rule put forward by the Crown is really, by my definition, the 60 per cent rule. You may agree or disagree about a few percentage points, and you may even agree or disagree on the subject of whether there should be any content regulations, but I think that all of us should have the right to make that determination within the law itself and not in some regulation or interpretation of the law that is not dealt with by parliament in this bill.
If my definition of a Canadian corporation does not constitute something that is Canadian, then what in the name of God would? That is really the question. In addition my amendment would allow a period of two years in which to comply. This would provide an opportunity for publications which wish to comply to divest themselves of their stock to Canadians, thus avoiding a fire sale or premature disposition of assets in a disorderly manner.
Surely that is not expecting too much when we have had magazines and periodicals in Canada operating under the law for many, many years. We should not turn around and kick them out of the country, or make them comply without giving them an adequate time frame in which to do so.
I have indicated also in my amendment that to qualify for the two-year period they must give a statement in writing to the minister showing their intent to comply within that two-year period. I think that is a very reasonable proposition. Some may argue that it should only be a
February 5, 1976

year or 18 months. I am game, but one thing I am not game for is that there is no time at all. I believe the approach I have outlined would in fact help guarantee a healthier Canadian magazine industry than the approach presently being proposed in Bill C-58.
Yesterday the Secretary of State in an interesting, quite informative, and very good speech, indicated the difficulty in respect of the possibility of split-runs that might occur in Canada if the not substantially the same as provision were interpreted as being less than 80 per cent. That is a good argument, and I must admit it gives me some concern. However, reducing the 80 per cent interpretation to 60 per cent in my view would not really cause that kind of problem.
I should indicate that the problem of split-runs does not exist in Canada today under the existing law, except in possible cases of U.S. publications which are already resident in Canada. It is the introduction of the new law, Bill C-58, that gives rise to the problem about which the minister seems concerned. It is not those who oppose this legislation who are creating this difficulty, but in fact those who propose Bill C-58.
I should also make a point in response to the observation by some in respect of the fear that Americans or others would come into Canada and take over the ownership of existing periodicals and, therefore, be able to have a hybrid magazine, half American and half Canadian. Surely I do not need to draw to the attention of the House the existence of the Foreign Investment Review Act. Surely we all know it is not possible to do that if it is concluded that it is not in the public interest to do so. So that is really a red herring as far as I am concerned.
I have grave reservations about the law in respect of the ministerial interpretation aspects. Many have expressed that reservation; none, however, have touched the central point of the real, legitimate objection to this question. I think it has been overlooked. Clearly it is advisable to have the essence of a bill within the bill itself wherever that is possible. We all agree with that.
Some have suggested that the Crown should not interpret the law. That to me is an absurdity, for how can the law be applied unless it is interpreted? The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) implied that and others have suggested it, but I will not debate that point. That is my understanding and I do not want to make an issue of it.
The essential role of the Department of Justice, in my view, is to assist the Crown in the interpretation and application of the law. The essential new factor being brought out in this legislation and in the interpretation of "not substantially the same as" is that the Crown is interpreting those words in such a manner as to achieve a policy objective, and is the Crown really entitled to do so?
Is, in fact, the Crown entitled to interpret the letter of the law against itself, interpret it in such a way as to render its literal meaning meaningless? I say, definitely not. Is it not the obligation of the Crown to interpret the law as it believes it would be interpreted by a court, as it believes that interpretation would be upheld by a court? The Crown, in my view, has chosen an interpretation to suit its own purposes, not an interpretation which it
Non-Canadian Publications
believes can be upheld. If it believed it could be upheld in court, why the suggestion that if it did not, we will change the law? This appears to me to be a departure totally contrary to the normal methods of application of the law.
On the contrary, in the case of expropriation, on which I have considerable experience, the law is interpreted in a very narrow and harsh way against the people under the umbrella that the Crown has no choice because it must follow the law like everyone else. Can the government of Canada have it both ways? If it is right to interpret "substantially the same as" to obtain a policy objective, then why can we not interpret the Expropriation Act to achieve justice rather than victimize the expropriated? Essentially, in a democratic society we should live under the law, not under the arbitrary rule of men. In the British system the law must stand or fall on its own words.
The Secretary of State implied an element of obstructionism in respect of this bill by some members of parliament. I must say that I do not feel guilty of that in any way. Indeed I have spoken out and I intend to continue to speak out on this bill. I have no intention of being silenced, but I have no intention either of delaying this bill to prohibit parliament from coming to a quick and speedy decision in respect of it.
I am delighted that Reader's Digest has indicated its ability to comply with the law. Like many others I wonder what really happened to make it possible. On June 4, 1975, I suggested my real and genuine concern for the uniqueness of Reader's Digest and its reprint operations in Canada. I am delighted, whether anybody admits it or not, that there appears to be a different application of this law in relationship to such types of magazines, and I am pleased that they can comply. I think most of us in this House would agree with that.
Now I want to make another point about an observation made in respect of the committee system. Some have indicated a genuine concern that the committee system fell down in terms of its application of Bill C-58. I do not basically feel that way. I think that the essential criticism in connection with the handling of Bill C-58 in the committee is that the government did something particularly and notably stupid. I believe that it is simply counter-productive, even in political terms, to deny at least some people who oppose a bill, if they happen to be on the government side, membership on a committee. A lot of the heat would have been taken off had this not occurred.

speechtext:
In conclusion, to close off this perhaps too lengthy speech, I should like to say that I oppose Bill C-58 as it presently stands unamended for the following reasons:
First, it does not achieve its objective of enhancing the Canadian periodical industry in any real or substantive way.
Second, it creates a false impression that it does so.
Third, it embodies a departure from the traditional means of legislating by having its fundamental application outside of the bill presently before parliament. On principle I cannot accept this approach.
Fourth, the consequence of its passage would create a near monopolistic situation in the publishing industry, which is against the public interest.
Fifth, it is a distortion of true cultural and economic nationalism. Essentially it extends the definition of Canadian to something other than that which is Canadian. Canadianism in this context is irrelevant, content becomes the relevant factor.
Sixth, its effective application will mean a net loss of jobs, job opportunities, and economic benefits to this country.
Seventh, it seeks not to give Canadian control over publishing activity in Canada, which is not now Canadian, but in fact makes it a virtue to force such Canadian subsidiaries of foreign publishers outside of Canada altogether rather than to Canadianize them.
Eighth, it would make more sense to Canadianize that which is in Canada than it does to bring forward a bill which has the potential of defining that which is Canadian as foreign. The real danger of this bill is that Macleans magazine could be considered a foreign periodical if it does not watch out.
Ninth, it would make more sense to assist positively the Canadian publication industry through positive action and the direction of more advertizing to it than it does to insulate it from competition and to guarantee for posterity a hothouse publication industry incapable of standing on its own feet in the world or in the marketplace.
Finally, its primary thrust is a holding out of false hopes to publishers and paying little or no attention to the interests of the consumers.
I urge that all members of the House support my proposed amendment. By doing so I believe that we shall improve the present legislation, bring the substantive provisions of the law under statute, resist passing a law in the interest of the elite against the interest of the many, substantially provide economic benefit to Canada, enhance
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
our employment opportunities for Canadian writers, and give more than lip service to the legitimate and genuine concerns expressed by the Canadian people.

Re: Income Tax Act and "Foreign" Publications
Thank you for your letter of 10 July, 1975 regarding changes in the tax legislation or enforcement policy proposed to be made in connection with "foreign" publications.
You will of course recall that we did not propose creation or continuation of special status for any magazine within the class of "foreign" or "domestic" publications. To these explanations there is a short (and technical) and a long (and principled) rebuttal.
[Mrs. Holt.)
The short answer is that the tax deductibility of an expense incurred for the purposed of earning income (e.g. advertising costs) is the normal rule. Deduction of expenses does not appear to us to be a "privilege" which the government of the day has allowed a business only where socially desirable aims are to be achieved by the outlay. Deductibility is the ordinary rule and not a "special advantage" as your Time and Reader's Digest press release suggests. Thus the content test which may result in non-deductibility for advertising in certain publications (which may be domestically owned and printed) creates an anomaly operating against those publications. It does not remove an anomaly which once favoured them.
More fundamentally however we must differ with you as to the aims to be promoted by content regulations. You appended to your letter to us a recent press release from your office quoting a passage from the O'Leary Report:
All members know it. They have seen it ad nauseam. I do not have to read it. They can get copies of it and read it.
Unfortunately we cannot consider the promotion of a "truly Canadian" outlook by the destruction of what have hitherto been publications supported by Canadian readers as other than censorship. Censorship in our understanding is content control or content manipulation by government.
I will repeat that, in case some members missed it.
Censorship in our understanding is content control or content manipulation by government. The O'Leary Report proposes manipulation of content to create a distinctive Canadian cultural identity. The current tax proposals (including the revival of enforcement of the 1965 content definition of foreign status) appear to adopt the O'Leary approach as government policy.
We do not know what aspect of content a future government, still disclaiming (as you do) any intention to censor, might see fit to consider in imposing taxation. A still more nationalistic administration might decide to define only writings about Canada as "domestic" for taxation purposes. A paternalistic government might decide that creation of jobs for Canadian writers was so high a priority that only Canadian citizens' work would rank as domestic. As civil libertarians we would not be concerned with what laudable motives might underlie either of these forms of content manipulation. Nor are we concerned with the policy of cultural renaissance which underlies the current government's policy. Our objection is to the intended results, not to the reason for seeking those results.
Before pressing through parliament legislation to accomplish this change in Canadian magazine content we ask you once again to consider whether the public choice of reading matter might not better be left to the market place.

David Barrett, who was the former NDP premier of British Columbia; Rosemary Brown, MLA, who was once runner up for the leadership and went quite far with the NDP party; Hugh Curtis, who is now Minister of Urban Affairs and Housing in British Columbia. There are mayors, men of the cloth, the Reverend R. R. Cunningham; the Hon. Judy LaMarsh, to name a name that is well known to many on this side of the House; Dr. Hugh Keenleyside, another well known figure, and on and on.
That is the end of the letter. The ramifications and obvious intent of Bill C-58 are frightening to me as a writer, as one who wants to read Time, not Time, U.S.A. with the Canadian content deleted.
As to all this talk about how we are free to get Time, how we can get Newsweek which has no special privileges, or perhaps Oui, or Playboy, or Penthouse, we are able to get
February 5, 1976

them, yes, but they didn't come to Canada, publish, give jobs, spend money here. I say, as one who believes Western Canada is not included as part of the national scene, because nationalism in Canada only extends about the fringes of Toronto, that perhaps those who are treating this bill lightly did not read the record of the Broadcasting Committee on Bill C-58 or understand the meaning of that dialogue.
When the Secretary of State and the senior officials of Revenue Canada tried to explain how they would measure content for the purpose of this legislation and how they would act as watchdogs over publications throughout the world-they might have to do that, they said, to be sure that the act would be followed-I was even more appalled at what the prospect of this bill would become. Phrases and rationalisations, perhaps even manipulations of truth, were quite remarkable and indicated the ridiculousness of trying to use the ruler of science or mathematics to measure culture and content.
Here are some of the remarkable phrases used in connection with content measurement: "continuing arrangements for access to material"; in other words, it isn't Canadian content, they don't care about Canadian writers in this bill. Norman Mailer could write, and the revenue people explained this. He could write in this magazine and be published and be acceptable. We are always protecting the publishers, not the writers and not those in allied trades. It must be "essentially different", whatever that means.
Then they talked of a "criterion for methodology" for measuring content. Then there were numerical interpretations which might be contributed to the word "substantial". It was a remarkable night, especially December 4, and I must say I did attend all the meetings. It was rather Gilbert and Sullivanesque, even Mack Sennett in many ways, except it was so serious.
Things like this happened. The man from Revenue, a senior civil servant who must answer the committee whether he believes in it or not, said, "If, for example, in our measurement we came up with 40 per cent it is arguable that it should have been 39 per cent, or 38 per cent, or 41 or 42 per cent, but apart from a minor margin of error we have not met any undue difficulties nor do we foresee any undue difficulty in measuring the arithmetic of the thing."
They are not getting a panel of editors, of journalists, of cultural experts to measure it. They are going to do it by a computer, or by one of those little pocket machines that add. They said there might be more difficulty in the area of "continuing arrangement" but it was felt desirable to insert this into the policy because otherwise officials of the Department of National Revenue would be expected to search all periodicals throughout the world to see whether a spot article was derived from something in Afghanistan-hear that: they have to go to Afghanistan to be sure it didn't happen there-or to Baluchistan, and I don't even know where that place is.
It is by establishing whether there is or is not a continuing arrangement that the matter becomes administrable. That is so fantastic as to be almost incomprehensible. If that were so, why every newspaper in Canada has a continuing arrangement with the New York Times, the Associated Press, United Press International, or Los
Non-Canadian Publications
Angeles Times writers. Even the University Press has a continuing arrangement. Who knows, they may develop a continuing arrangement with Xavier Hollander.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: Explain!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
That is for you to explain, gentlemen!
When the witnesses at that committee meetings were trying to explain "substantially different" and "continuing relation" in order to hit this target, they obviously fluttered around. They could only miss the bull's eye, Reader's Digest, Time, etc. which they were out to get. There is no doubt in my mind that when the rules changed from May 5 to October 23, and finally in the last week to make a special privilege for Reader's Digest, which in a few years will return to haunt Reader's Digest in a new Bill 58, the objectives were clear.
They will hit the whole outer edge of the target and not just Reader's Digest and Time, all foreign news and features, even the comics, except for Ben Wicks' little item. They seem not to realize that they will be the victims. Those are the dangerous ramifications I urge you to reject. When you play with content you endanger the freedom of choice to publish, you endanger the freedom of availability of culture.
One of Vancouver's most eminent writers, an international author and journalist, Lisa Hobbs, responded to a statement made in Vancouver at the opening of the CBC building by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). The hon. gentleman had stated:
We can't compete if Canadian interests are left to their own initiatives. Do they (people) want us simply to become a total U.S. cultural satellite? We have to recognise that we must work against that eventuality. And in the leadership of that effort must be the Canadian government.
Lisa Hobbs asked:
How would this "leadership" be expressed? According to Mr. Faulkner, in "controlling the importation of foreign culture." It is a nice phrase. It means denying us access to it, which means censorship. And it rings with the echo of the boot. There is no free society in the world today that censors publishing and the arts.
The minister announced at the committee hearings that he had a cultural plan for Canada. Once before in history a government announced a cultural plan in the name of nationalism. That government called itself "National Socialist". It is kind of frightening that the socialists here are also nationalists. I stand up today and speak against my government, with sadness but with intensity, because I know the end result of cultural planning. I am not as young as all the rest of you here, and I remember. I am just an amateur here but I've got gears! I remember that in the name of nationalism books were burnt and that, in the striving for purity of race and nationalism, millions died. I do not want even to start to set in motion any form of controls that can lose us our freedom.
Another very disturbing aspect that the CBC has uncovered is the power of Canadian publishers in Canada. Every writer of books knows very well that it is the publisher who makes the money. Anyone who tells a Canadian author that he can get rich, even with a best seller, is trying to deceive him, especially if the Canadian publisher

February 5, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
is absorbed in making a few of the eastern idols even richer. I say that from personal knowledge. Every author is but part of the publisher's stable and few ever making a living out of books. It is the publisher who makes the money if you have a best seller for him; he only cares about the buck. Oh, they love their authors-as long as they write and allow use of their names.
I should like to mention another interesting point, something that has gone on for a great length of time, not something for which this particular government is responsible. Perhaps even the leaders of hon. gentlemen opposite started it, or some senior civil servants. I am never sure who is running my life around here.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: The whip.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
The whip is a great man. He smiles at me even when he knows I am not doing quite the thing he would like me to do. If anyone is thinking of becoming a Canadian writer, whether he be a journalist or an editorial writer, let them forget it because no one cares about them.
The Department of External Affairs has played a strange game in all of this. The Canadian embassies' reading rooms and libraries will not accept works of Canadian authors unless they are published by Canadian publishing houses. There were many outstanding Canadian writers for Macmillan Publishing, but their books could not qualify for Canadian embassies. Maclean-Hunter bought out Macmillan and they suddenly became Canadian, their publications could go into embassies and much money was spent on them, for which they received royalties. Canadians who write for Ryerson lost their Canadian identity as far as external affairs' reading rooms were concerned as soon as the publishing house was bought out by Americans. How petty, how ridiculous, and how unnationalistic that is.
I hope that as of today the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) will end this discrimination against Canadian authors who choose to publish where they will. I personally am a Canadian author, not because I was born in Canada but because I happen to publish with a Canadian publisher. But I will not be publishing with a Canadian publisher in future oecause I think American subsidiaries care about us westerners, about Canadian culture and writers, just a little more than the Toronto mafia.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: I hope those socialists are listening.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
As I say, it is ironic that the content control is not designed to protect Canadian writers. It does nothing for Canadian publishing. Everything it does is for the publisher, the billionaire conglomerates. Southam's are linked with Maclean's in many enterprises and they are pulling out their foreign correspondents. There are only two foreign correspondents in Peking offices to cover the situation in China. In other words, if continuing content is to be the rule we will not be getting any foreign news from China because we can only get it through a continuing arrangement with Associated Press and all the other agencies.
The history of Bill C-58 makes me think of a king who is in a card game and cannot stand to lose. He changes the rules as he goes along. He becomes ridiculous and the game not worth the playing. I wonder though if even that king

would tear up the cards or ultimately assassinate his opponent when the rules are changed so much that they come full circle to start again.
The rules in this bill have been changed several times. On May 5 the requirement was that half the content was to be "new, fresh, original material which has not appeared in any periodica] outside Canada". Obviously that strange dictum had one purpose, and it was a dangerous purpose. Perhaps it was written by an accountant rather than a person of culture-perhaps a schoolteacher. No one can really define "new, fresh, original material". I defy anyone to tell me what that is. Perhaps the Secretary of State has never heard it said that there is nothing new under the sun. Perhaps there is nothing really fresh or original either.
To show the danger of this whole exercise, when it was discovered that Time was ready to meet the May 5 dictum the "king" quickly changed the rules and on October 23 content suddenly was no longer 50 per cent but 80 per cent. Now it has been changed again. One victim is now saved, Reader's Digest, and its French edition Selection. I can only suspect that this was the result of political expediency. Perhaps a few members on this side can accept that kind of deal, but I cannot because of the danger of the principle involved. It is not acceptable to me, and I doubt whether Reader's Digest will be able to face the repercussions of once more being accused of being given special privileges.
This is reminiscent of a strange event in the prohibition era. When the United States could not get A1 Capone for the substantive offences of murder and bootlegging, they got him on income tax evasion. Canada is doing the same thing here in order to rid the community of Reader's Digest, Time, MD, and KVOS Bellingham and other border stations. Other small publications will also become victims. But none of these are criminals. They are not the A1 Capones of culture. On the contrary, they are good corporate citizens, perhaps too moral for the swingers who saw Reader's Digest, during the bead and beard hippie era, as a symbol of despised morality and Time as the symbol of patriotism in the Viet Nam explosion.
If law is written to cure an imagined ailment-a sort of sociological hypochrondia, perhaps a cultural hypochondria, imagined and not real- by the Department of the Secretary of State, using the Department of Revenue as its tool, it can only end negatively and dangerously.
The dangers to freedom of choice and the spin-offs from that have been referred to already. It is difficult for me to conceive of any government, any body of people, assigned to this very serious duty we have been given by the electorate, creating law here that is not positive, is not for the good of the majority and the nation, but is built on a negative, an anti-American bias.
I should like to challenge anyone in this House to put on those scales of justice what will be gained for Canada and Canadians by this action, and what will be lost. They will find little if anything of gain, and the loss will rock the scale off its base.
February 5, 1976
