subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-SUGGESTION THAT PROVISION FOR EQUALITY OF SEXES WITH REGARD TO INCOME BE MADE MANDATORY
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-SUGGESTION THAT PROVISION FOR EQUALITY OF SEXES WITH REGARD TO INCOME BE MADE MANDATORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to get as much as I can into my seven minutes on this very important issue. Approximately one third of the Canadian work force is made up of women, and almost all of that total, some 2 million, are subjected to job discrimination in terms of the income they are paid. All the rhetoric and supposed efforts of the government to one side, considering what the government has attempted or is alleged to have attempted in the past ten years, instead of the gap between women's and men's income narrowing in that past decade it has widened.
The most recent statistical information provided by the women's bureau within the federal Department of Labour, published in this year, indicates that the wage and salary position of women in the Canadian labour force during the past decade has become worse and not better. The average pay for a woman now is 60 per cent of that of a man doing the same job.
Fully two thirds of women in the work force are doing four categories of work, namely, clerical, sales, service, and professional. The one group, and I think this is understandable, that has made some progress in recent years has been the professional group. I am sure all Canadians and members in all parties will be pleased at that fact, but will not be so pleased about the other fact, and that is that with respect to the other categories of women their average income position has worsened.
Let me present to the House four illustrations of the current situation in respect of women's incomes as compared to men's. These figures again come from the Department of Labour and are the most recent, being for the year 1973. The first category is hospital workers and medical lab technologists. The average monthly pay for a woman was $659, and for a man $693. For hotels employing 200 or more people, men earned on the average of $464 a month, and women $427. In real estate, clerical and related workers, women earned on the average $3.25 an hour compared to $3.82 for men. In banks and financial institutions, for those
Adjournment Debate
who were in a supervisory position, as of 1973, women earned on the average $4.39 per hour, as compared to $5.67 for men. In clerical positions in the same financial institutions women averaged $3.15 a hour, and men once again subtantially more, $3.94.
One could go on with a whole variety of average and low income occupations and show the remarkable and sad discrepancy which exists between men's and women's salaries in 1975. The government, in terms of its program for International Women's year, last year spent a lot of money, but in the main spent money on glib advertising campaigns, in my view, and on rather sexist slogans such as "Why Not?" and "Pourquoi non?", but did almost nothing in terms of removing the discrepancy which exists by taking concrete steps in national terms. I am not talking about federal employees only, but in national terms the government took almost no measures to remove that discrepancy in income which exists between working men and women.
There was one opportunity which would have enabled the federal government to show in a demonstrable way its serious concern about the situation in recent months, and that was of course the anti-inflation legislation. As the minister knows, there is a specific exemption from the guidelines provided in the legislation which would enable employers in Canada to go beyond the guidelines for wages and salary increases if the purpose were "to eliminate sex discrimination in pay practices". That is a laudable exemption provided in the legislation. It would have been more laudable, I suggest, if the government had followed up once again with something other than the permissive phrase that is in the legislation and had actually taken steps to implement seriously that possibility which it leaves open to employers. There was nothing in the regulations that I was able to see pertaining to this fact following the passage of the legislation.
The government has done nothing in terms of publicity to private employers stressing the moral obligation- because it is not within federal jurisdiction but in a provincial area where most people are employed-that private employers should now have to eliminate this unjust and outdated discrimination.
There is nothing that I am aware of that the federal government has done in terms of its negotiations with the provinces to persuade, cajole, or coerce in some way the provinces to take direct steps to implement on a mandatory basis this permissive clause in the anti-inflation program. I repeat that it would have been a glorious opportunity for the government to try to implement within the framework of its anti-inflation legislation a policy which in 1976 could have led to the virtual elimination of wage and salary discrimination between men and women in Canada. I suggest that it is a step which is long overdue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-SUGGESTION THAT PROVISION FOR EQUALITY OF SEXES WITH REGARD TO INCOME BE MADE MANDATORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was fascinated to hear the hon. gentleman say that the best way to conduct federal-provincial relations was to coerce the provinces. I suppose he would adopt as the NDP slogan "coercive federalism".
I have already replied in substance to the question on male-female earning differentials raised by the hon. member. The government's position is two-fold: first, it has
2 1 130-55

February 5, 1976
Adjournment Debate
taken steps to correct the situation insofar as workers under its jurisdiction are concerned, and secondly, it very much hopes, although it cannot impose its view, that other jurisdictions will follow its example. I would like to elaborate briefly on these two points.
With respect to workers under federal jurisdiction the necessary steps have been taken to ensure that women receive equal pay. In line with the publication in 1970 of the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the government has placed before the House legislation which will, among other things, add sex and marital status as prohibited grounds for discrimination under the Canada Labour Code. I am referring here, of course, to Bill C-72 which is now before the House.
As for other workers, that is to say, those not under federal jurisdiction, labour standards applying to them are those under the various provincial labour codes. The hon. member is certainly aware that the anti-inflation legislation was not intended, nor would it be legally able to amend the provincial labour laws. While the government is aware of and respects the jurisdictional constraints, it has been conscious of the need to create an environment which would facilitate the resolution of such problems. That is why the white paper on the anti-inflation program states, and I quote:
... employers may also grant increases in compensation above the guidelines if such increases result from taking measures ... to eliminate sex discrimination in pay practices.
In brief, the government believes it has played an important role in creating a climate which will help in the resolution of male-female pay differentials. It has done so in a spirit of respect for jurisdictional allocation of powers in Canada and by consciously designed provisions both in the anti-inflation guidelines and Bill C-72 in carrying out its own responsibilities. We are confident that with these actions the general situation will continue to improve.

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-SUGGESTED MORATORIUM ON IMPOSITION OF FEE
NATIONAL PARKS-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-SUGGESTED MORATORIUM ON IMPOSITION OF FEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I last raised the question of the Prince Edward Island national park with the minister I was depressed and distressed by his answer. I noted with much regret that he was applauded by members of the Liberal party when he said, and I quote:
Basically, the position is that the national park in Prince Edward Island is one of our national parks and part of our national system. It is very difficult to say we are not going to charge a fee for Prince Edward Island but will for Fundy and Kejimkujik. It is part of our national system and we feel it is equitable that the users should be contributing a minimum of 18 per cent, which is what is amounts to, of the operating costs of our national parks.
I think that unless and until he recognizes that there are differences as among parks and among provinces, the minister will not approach an equitable solution to this serious problem. The history of this dominion has shown that Confederation has been one long series of adjustments and readjustments.
It was a century ago that John A. Macdonald and Joseph Howe worked out financial changes in the BNA Act
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).J
respecting Nova Scotia, a province which on Dominion Day, 1867, had voted solidly, indeed almost unanimously, for the anti-confederate ticket. Only Charles Tupper escaped the wrath of the electors.
Ever since there have been special formulae worked out. No realistic person could expect a nation composed of provinces of such great differences in size, wealth and economic and social values to work in an inflexible framework. Compromise and common sense are the essential ingredients of a functioning federation or confederation.
While speaking of special provisions, arrangements or inhibitions, I might mention one we do not like. It is no delight to Prince Edward Island or the island portion of Newfoundland to know that they alone must pay to go to or to come from another province. I wonder how the residents of Saskatchewan and Manitoba would like to pay a toll every time they move from province to province.
I appeal once more, most earnestly and sincerely, to the minister to listen to the people, the legislature, and the government of Prince Edward Island. The sea has been our inspiration throughout our history. It has also and often been our economic strength. Consider how much of our coast line was given over to the national park. Realize that the imposition of this fee is really cutting off island people from their ancient joy and heritage, the beauty, majesty, and charm of the glittering sea.
If some day soon you, sir, or the charming parliamentary secretary, come to my province and I offer to take you fishing for that queen of the sea, the mackerel, I will have to pay to get into the fishing grounds, and that might stagger my Presbyterian thrift.
In all my years in public life, and they are now quite a few, I have never seen such depth of feeling as exists in Prince Edward Island in respect to this question. I urge that some arrangements be made, whether the establishment of a new concept of a sea shore park as there is in the United States, or whatever. Let the minister indicate his awareness of our unique situation and bring about a fair and acceptable adjustment to it.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-SUGGESTED MORATORIUM ON IMPOSITION OF FEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would gladly reciprocate with an invitation to go fishing for some west coast salmon off the Queen Charlotte Islands if we were fortunate enough to have any national parks in that part of Canada. Unfortunately that is not the case.
I really do regret that the hon. member has been depressed and distressed that Prince Edward Island must pay as other Canadians must pay for the privilege of enjoying national parks. The only difference to date has been that other provinces in the west have paid for the privilege of utilizing parks for 40 years. Suddenly the eastern part of Canada has begun to take on its share of the future improvements.
The minister has listened to the people very carefully. They want park facilities and good ones; they want improvements and developments and these things must be paid for. Unfortunately in today's economy they must be paid for by the people who utilize them. It is a most natural human reaction to seek to avoid paying fees.
February 5, 1976

The decision to increase national parks motor licence fees and apply them where they had not been collected before, was taken in 1974. It arose from the minister's efforts to embark on a major program of development, to establish new parks, to provide basic facilities in new parks, and to preserve and protect more of Canada's natural and historic heritage of which the hon. member speaks with such eloquence.
The rapid expansion in the number of national parks within recent years on a very limited budget was in many instances done at the expense of the old established parks in the system, such as Prince Edward Island national park. Unfortunately, this happened over a period when ten new parks came into being, and there has not been sufficient funding to develop them all at one time without the participation of the people who make use of them. I know the hon. member would not wish to shirk the duty of the people of Prince Edward Island in supplying their assistance to parks of Canada in their growth and development. Maybe with the help of the people of Prince Edward Island the people on the Queen Charlotte Islands will have a park one day.

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL AID TO REPAIR STORM DAMAGE IN NEW BRUNSWICK
FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL AID TO REPAIR STORM DAMAGE IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this country is a confederation of provinces into a single unit. It was formed with the understanding that the provinces, as they became members of this structure, recognized that there were mutual responsibilities of one province to another, of one region to another, and of the national government to all provinces and all regions.
In recent years the tendencies of the national government has been to disclaim responsibilities which are historically inherent in the principles of confederation. Examples of this national responsibility can be cited from the construction of the national railroad, the construction of a series of airports for air travel, the construction of the Trans-Canada highway, the assumption of responsibility for the maintenance, construction, and expansion of the seaports as well as those ports of national consequence on the inland water system of Canada. And one can go on over a long list of items which are examples of the assumption of responsibility by the national government where an individual province or region could not, without undue hardship assume responsibility for the particular situation in which it found itself.
That coastal area of Canada which forms the Bay of Fundy now finds itself in a disaster position; whether it be in the area of Yarmouth or Grand Manan, whether it be Saint John or Moncton, and the area deserves relief from the Government of Canada on a disaster basis.
While I was encouraged yesterday by the answer of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) given to the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), I was most discouraged by the answer from the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) in his reply to me today. The Prime Minister recognized in a heartening way that this is not a situation which would make a recurring claim upon the national treasury. In contrast to this, as I remember his remarks, the Minister of State (Fisheries) today said that
Adjournment Debate
only if something were started by the provinces would any relief be forthcoming.
In view of the fact that this cabinet minister is a resident of New Brunswick and is looked upon as the voice of the province of New Brunswick in cabinet, it was indeed disheartening to hear that the damages to the industry for which he is responsible will only receive relief upon initiation of the individual provinces concerned. This is the second occasion since he has been minister responsible for fisheries that he has turned a deaf ear to the pleas from people in dire trouble.
During the fall of 1975 a multitude of fishermen on the Atlantic coast suffered serious damage as a result of unusual weather, and their plea for help went unanswered. Some of the same people have again experienced disastrous losses, particularly lobster fishermen, within a time span of less than six months. This type of loss is beyond their means; yet the returns from this industry are of major importance to the national economy.
I am sure that when the Prime Minister made his statement that this area could receive consideration under the existing circumstances, he was aware of the fact that though the policy of government has not been to recognize problems such as this, they have not chosen to declare a disaster area on their own initiative and the machinery is still in place to permit this to be done. Though the position of the Minister of State responsible for Fisheries was historically correct, during the past few years on the basis of existing government policy the machinery is still in place whereby special funds could be allocated to alleviate the difficulties of that storm ravaged area. The statutory authority for this is still in existence, although it has not been in use.
The people of the cities and towns which have been so thoroughly disrupted must be congratulated upon the dispatch with which they have dealt with their problems. The co-operation of the residents with one another in the city of Saint John would restore the faith of mankind in the principle of brotherly love. It is a stirring example of the practice of the good neighbour principle.
I wonder does the minister recognize that the livelihood of hundreds of families and their life savings have been eliminated in the span of a very few hours of almost merciless weather. I wonder how many people in this House realize that this was just not an ordinary storm. This was a storm which had winds of hurricane proportions. This was a storm in which wind measuring instruments registered velocities of more than 120 miles per hour on a continuing basis. These were not just momentary gusts. Boats do not get thrown across highways and into a wooded area by a single gust of wind. Fish processing buildings are not lifted off their foundations and scattered by a single gust of wind. This was a storm which carried continuing winds of hurricane proportions and the damage is in direct relation to their intensity.
Canada has had a record of generosity on an international basis. It has always come to the aid of those areas which suffered catastrophes. I am sure we will come to the aid of Guatemala, to some degree, after the moments of horror people there have experienced and the catastrophic
2 I 1 30-5 514

February 5, 1976
Adjournment Debate
damage to man and his property. If we do not, we should; but we should be equally aware of the needs of our own people in time of trouble. It is not proper that the Government of Canada, or any of its ministers, should say that this is a provincial or a regional problem. It is, instead, only fair and right that government should say that this is indeed an unusual circumstance and that we shall indeed come to the aid of those who need it so badly.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal proposed that a formula should be adopted by the government under which. The first dollar, per capita, of a province required to reimburse for flood or other types of unusual damage should come from the province. The second dollar spent within a province for this purpose should be shared equally by the Government of Canada and the province. The third dollar spent for this purpose should be absorbed 75 per cent by the Government of Canada and 25 per cent by the province concerned. The fourth dollar and each additional dollar per capita of a province required for this purpose should be financed by at least a 90 per cent contribution from the federal government.
The adoption of such a program would certainly relieve the present situation immensely. It would be a step in the right direction. It might very well be a very proper and responsible position for the Government of Canada to take on a national basis. It would certainly be preferable to the formula which presently exists. It would not, however, relieve the Government of Canada of the responsibility of an immediate assessment of the damage to a national industry, such as that of the salt water fishing industry.
I am, and I always have been, of the opinion that unusual expenditure by any area of Canada should be the responsibility of the Government of Canada in recognition of the differences in the various areas of our country and the unique responsibilities which some areas have but which others do not have at all.
I thank the Prime Minister for his sympathetic statement and I implore the Minister of State (Fisheries), in view of this statement, to assess immediately the damage in the Atlantic area and sell to cabinet a proposal for furnishing adequate money to re-establish those who cannot re-establish themselves, whether they live along the shore or inland. I wish to put in a special word for those who live along the shore, who are engaged in a profession which few of us choose as our source of income and who, through generations of almost unendurable conditions, have made such a major contribution to our total economy. They are not asking for charity. They are asking for the recognition of a right which is truly theirs. They ask their government in Ottawa to recognize their plight and lend the necessary assistance to alleviate it.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL AID TO REPAIR STORM DAMAGE IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is doing exactly what the hon. gentleman is requesting.
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) yesterday received the assurance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that his office is looking into the possibility, if I quote him correctly, of providing an exception in this case and studying the situation in a sympathetic way.
In reply to further questioning today by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte, the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) gave his assurance that officials of his department would co-operate and help the province assess the damage as far as fisheries are concerned. Therefore, to the two requests that the hon. member made, he received assurances from the Prime Minister and the Minister of State (Fisheries).
I understand that today surveys were being conducted by the government of New Brunswick together with EMO and, we hope, the assistance of the federal fisheries officers.

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL AID TO REPAIR STORM DAMAGE IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext: "We hope." So do I.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL AID TO REPAIR STORM DAMAGE IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
The hon. member was given assurance today by the Minister of State (Fisheries). I do not know what else he wants.
As the hon. member stated, the existing formula is that the province has to put in the first dollar of capital, the second and third dollars would be funded 50 per cent by the federal government, the fourth and fifth dollars by the federal government, and the excess 90 per cent by the federal government. That has been the exact formula since 1970 for every single case with a few exceptions of small disasters that were very localized. However, as the hon. member stated, this was a large disaster.
Through the efforts of the hon. member and those of other hon. members affected, the Prime Minister has taken this exceptional step. However, let me assure him that under the existing formula the initiative for the assessing of damages for disaster relief rests with the provincial governments. It has always rested there. As I stated, the hon. member's comments have been taken into account by the Prime Minister and the Minister of State (Fisheries). I think at the moment that is all we can expect from the government.
